## Console Commands

> **Manage audit data via the command line**

> [!NOTE]
> These commands are provided by **[auditor-doctrine-provider](https://damienharper.github.io/auditor-docs/auditor-doctrine-provider)** (not auditor core).
> For programmatic usage and standalone registration, see [Schema Management](https://damienharper.github.io/auditor-docs/auditor-doctrine-provider/providers/doctrine/schema).

When using auditor-bundle or the standalone `auditor-doctrine-provider`, these console commands are available:

### 📋 Available Commands

| Command                  | Description                                          |
|--------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|
| `audit:schema:update`    | Create or update audit tables to the current schema  |
| `audit:schema:migrate`   | Migrate legacy v1 audit tables to schema v2          |
| `audit:clean`            | Remove old audit entries                             |
| `audit:snapshot`         | Record the current state of existing entities        |
| `audit:export`           | Export audit entries as NDJSON, JSON or CSV          |
| `audit:roots:rebuild`    | Index existing entries under their audit roots       |

### 🛠️ `audit:schema:update`

Creates new audit tables and updates existing ones to match the current schema.

#### Usage

```bash
php bin/console audit:schema:update [options]
```

#### Options

| Option       | Short | Description                                          |
|--------------|-------|------------------------------------------------------|
| `--dump-sql` |       | Show SQL statements without executing them           |
| `--force`    | `-f`  | Execute the SQL statements                           |

#### Examples

```bash
# Preview the SQL that would be executed
php bin/console audit:schema:update --dump-sql

# Output:
# The following SQL statements will be executed:
#
#     CREATE TABLE users_audit (...);
#     CREATE INDEX idx_type_xxx ON users_audit (type);
#     ...

# Execute the changes
php bin/console audit:schema:update --force

# Both: show SQL and execute
php bin/console audit:schema:update --dump-sql --force
```

#### When to Run

Run this command:

- After adding `#[Auditable]` to a new entity
- After updating auditor to a new version
- During deployment to ensure schema is up-to-date

> [!TIP]
> The command is safe to run multiple times. Existing tables are updated (not recreated), existing data is preserved, and only necessary changes are applied.

#### Exit Codes

| Code | Meaning                                          |
|------|--------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | Success (including "nothing to update")          |
| 1    | Error or missing required options                |

### 🔄 `audit:schema:migrate`

Migrates legacy v1 audit tables to schema v2 (ULID `transaction_id`, unified `blame` JSON column).
Safe to run multiple times; skips already-migrated tables.

> [!CAUTION]
> `audit:schema:update` refuses to run while any audit table still has the legacy v1 schema.
> Always run `audit:schema:migrate --force` first when upgrading from auditor-bundle 7.x or earlier.

#### Usage

```bash
php bin/console audit:schema:migrate [options]
```

#### Options

| Option                       | Description                                                  |
|------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| `--dump-sql`                 | Show SQL statements without executing them                   |
| `--force`, `-f`              | Execute the migration                                        |
| `--convert-all`              | Convert transaction hashes and diffs in one pass (recommended) |
| `--convert-transaction-hash` | Convert SHA-1 `transaction_hash` values to ULID format       |
| `--convert-diffs`            | Convert legacy diffs JSON to the v2 envelope format          |
| `--limit=N`                  | Convert `N` transactions or rows only, keep the legacy columns (resumable), print an estimate of the remaining time |
| `--drop-transaction-hash`    | ⚠️ Drop `transaction_hash` **without** converting it: legacy rows lose their transaction grouping for good |

#### Examples

```bash
# Preview the DDL that would be executed
php bin/console audit:schema:migrate --dump-sql

# Full migration in one pass (recommended)
php bin/console audit:schema:migrate --force --convert-all

# Estimate the duration on a copy of the production data
php bin/console audit:schema:migrate --force --convert-all --limit=10000
```

---

### 🧹 `audit:clean`

Removes audit entries older than a specified retention period.

#### Usage

```bash
php bin/console audit:clean [options] [keep]
```

#### Arguments

| Argument | Default | Description                                           |
|----------|---------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| `keep`   | `P12M`  | Retention period as ISO 8601 duration                 |

#### Options

| Option         | Short | Description                                        |
|----------------|-------|----------------------------------------------------|
| `--no-confirm` |       | Skip confirmation prompt                           |
| `--dry-run`    |       | Show what would be deleted without executing       |
| `--dump-sql`   |       | Show the SQL statements                            |
| `--date`       | `-d`  | Clean audits before a specific date                |
| `--exclude`    | `-x`  | Exclude specific entities (can be used multiple times) |
| `--include`    | `-i`  | Include only specific entities (can be used multiple times) |

#### Retention Period Format

The `keep` argument uses ISO 8601 duration format:

| Format  | Meaning              |
|---------|----------------------|
| `P12M`  | 12 months            |
| `P1Y`   | 1 year               |
| `P6M`   | 6 months             |
| `P30D`  | 30 days              |
| `P7D`   | 7 days               |
| `P1D`   | 1 day                |
| `PT12H` | 12 hours             |

#### Per-Entity Retention Policies

An entity can define its own retention policy, either with `#[Auditable]` or in the bundle configuration
(see the `auditor-bundle` documentation):

```php
use DH\Auditor\Attribute\Auditable;

#[Auditable(maxAge: 'P7Y')]               // keep 7 years of history
class Payment {}

#[Auditable(maxEntries: 10_000)]          // keep the 10,000 most recent entries
class Session {}

#[Auditable(maxAge: 'P1Y', maxEntries: 500)]
class User {}
```

- `maxAge` is an ISO 8601 duration greater than zero; `maxEntries` is a positive integer. Invalid values make the
  attribute fail as soon as it is loaded.
- For an entity with a `maxAge`, that value **replaces** the global cutoff (`keep` argument or `--date` option),
  whether it is shorter or longer.
- Entities without a `maxAge` keep using the global cutoff, exactly as before.
- `maxEntries` applies on top of the age rule: an entry is deleted when it is older than the cutoff **or** not among
  the `maxEntries` most recent entries of the entity (most recent first, ties broken by insertion order).
- With single-table inheritance, the classes of a hierarchy share one audit table: each rule only deletes the
  entries of its own class (`discriminator` column). Entries without a discriminator are left untouched.
- Every policy is validated before anything is deleted: one invalid policy makes the command fail without
  deleting anything.
- Cutoffs are computed in the auditor timezone (the one audit entries are written in).

The policies in use are listed before the confirmation prompt:

```
Per-entity retention policies (they override the global cutoff for these entities):
 --------------------- --------- -------------
  Entity                Max age   Max entries
 --------------------- --------- -------------
  App\Entity\Payment    P7Y       -
  App\Entity\Session    -         10000
 --------------------- --------- -------------
```

#### Examples

##### Basic Cleanup

```bash
# Keep last 12 months (default)
php bin/console audit:clean

# Keep last 6 months
php bin/console audit:clean P6M

# Keep last 30 days
php bin/console audit:clean P30D
```

##### Preview Mode

```bash
# See what would be deleted without actually deleting
php bin/console audit:clean P6M --dry-run

# See the SQL statements
php bin/console audit:clean P6M --dump-sql
```

##### Non-Interactive

```bash
# Skip confirmation (useful for cron jobs)
php bin/console audit:clean P12M --no-confirm
```

##### Custom Date

```bash
# Delete audits before a specific date
php bin/console audit:clean --date=2024-01-01

# Combine with no-confirm for scripts
php bin/console audit:clean --date=2023-12-31 --no-confirm
```

##### Entity Filtering

```bash
# Exclude specific entities from cleanup
php bin/console audit:clean -x App\\Entity\\User -x App\\Entity\\Payment

# Include only specific entities
php bin/console audit:clean -i App\\Entity\\Log -i App\\Entity\\Session

# Long form
php bin/console audit:clean --exclude=App\\Entity\\User --include=App\\Entity\\Post
```

#### Output

```
You are about to clean audits created before 2024-01-15 14:30:45: 12 classes involved.
 Do you want to proceed? (yes/no) [no]:
 > yes

Starting...
Cleaning audit tables... (users_audit)
 12/12 [============================] 100%
Cleaning audit tables... (done)

 [OK] Success.
```

#### Scheduling

For automated cleanup, add to your crontab:

```bash
# Clean up audits older than 12 months, daily at 2 AM
0 2 * * * /path/to/php /path/to/bin/console audit:clean P12M --no-confirm >> /var/log/audit-clean.log 2>&1
```

With `auditor-bundle`, pruning can also be scheduled with Symfony Scheduler (opt-in, see the bundle configuration).
Unlike `audit:clean`, a scheduled run only applies explicit retention policies: entities without a policy are left
untouched unless a default max age is configured.

> [!TIP]
> Use Symfony Messenger Scheduler if available for more robust scheduling.

#### Exit Codes

| Code | Meaning                        |
|------|--------------------------------|
| 0    | Success or cancelled by user   |
| 1    | Error                          |

### 📸 `audit:snapshot`

Records the current state of existing entities in their audit tables. Run it once auditing is enabled on a
database that already holds data: the history of each entity then starts with its state at that time
instead of its first change.

#### Usage

```bash
php bin/console audit:snapshot [options] [--] [<entities>...]
```

#### Arguments

| Argument   | Description                                      |
|------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| `entities` | Audited entities to snapshot (FQCN), or `--all`  |

#### Options

| Option         | Short | Default | Description                                                     |
|----------------|-------|---------|-----------------------------------------------------------------|
| `--all`        | `-a`  |         | Snapshot every audited entity                                   |
| `--batch-size` | `-b`  | `500`   | Entities read and written per database transaction              |
| `--force`      | `-f`  |         | Also snapshot entities that already have an audit history       |
| `--dry-run`    |       |         | Count the entities to snapshot, write nothing                   |

#### What is written

One `insert` entry per entity, whose diffs carry `"snapshot": true` (`Entry::isSnapshot()` returns `true`):
every audited field with `old: null` and its current value as `new`, as for an insertion. Its `created_at`
is the date of the snapshot and its blame is the console user.

Entities that already have an audit entry are skipped, so the command can be run again safely.
To-many associations are not snapshotted, and enabled Doctrine filters (e.g. soft-delete) apply.

#### Examples

```bash
# Preview: how many entities would be snapshotted
php bin/console audit:snapshot --all --dry-run

# Snapshot two entities
php bin/console audit:snapshot 'App\Entity\Post' 'App\Entity\Author'

# Snapshot everything with bigger batches
php bin/console audit:snapshot --all --batch-size=2000
```

#### Exit Codes

| Code | Meaning                                         |
|------|-------------------------------------------------|
| 0    | Success (or already running)                    |
| 1    | Error (e.g. entity not audited)                 |
| 2    | Invalid arguments                               |

### 📤 `audit:export`

Exports audit entries as NDJSON (default, recommended for large exports), JSON or CSV, streamed to the standard
output or to a file. Each line or row is an `Entry::toArray()`.

```bash
php bin/console audit:export [options] [entity]
```

| Option        | Description                                              |
|---------------|----------------------------------------------------------|
| `entity`      | Entity FQCN to export, all auditable entities by default |
| `--id`        | Filter by object ID                                      |
| `--from`      | Entries created on or after this date (ISO 8601)         |
| `--to`        | Entries created on or before this date (ISO 8601)        |
| `--blame-id`  | Filter by user ID                                        |
| `--format`    | `ndjson` (default), `json` or `csv`                      |
| `--anonymize` | Mask the user and IP fields                              |
| `--output`    | Write to this file instead of the standard output        |

```bash
php bin/console audit:export App\\Entity\\Post --format=csv --from=2026-01-01 --output=posts.csv
```

---

### 🌳 `audit:roots:rebuild`

Indexes the existing audit entries under their audit roots (`#[AuditRoot]`), after declaring a new root or after
migrating audit tables to schema v2. Only missing index rows are written, so the command can be run again.

```bash
php bin/console audit:roots:rebuild [--entity=FQCN ...] [--dry-run]
```

See [Histories](../history.md) and the
[Doctrine provider history page](https://damienharper.github.io/auditor-docs/auditor-doctrine-provider/querying/history#rebuilding-the-index).

---

### 🔒 Command Locking

These commands use Symfony's Lock component to prevent concurrent execution:

```
The command is already running in another process.
```

> [!NOTE]
> This ensures data integrity when running commands in parallel or from cron jobs.

### ✅ Best Practices

1. **Always preview first** - Use `--dump-sql` and `--dry-run` before executing
2. **Backup before cleanup** - Especially for large deletions
3. **Schedule regular cleanups** - Prevent unlimited growth
4. **Monitor disk space** - Audit tables can grow quickly
5. **Consider retention policies** - Different entities may need different retention
6. **Test in staging** - Verify commands work as expected before production

### 🔧 Troubleshooting

#### "The command is already running"

> [!WARNING]
> Wait for the other instance to finish, or check for stuck processes.

#### Schema update has no changes

> [!NOTE]
> This means your audit tables are already up-to-date.

#### Permission denied

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Ensure the database user has CREATE TABLE and ALTER TABLE permissions.

#### Timeout during large cleanup

For very large tables, consider:
- Running during off-peak hours
- Increasing PHP timeout
- Breaking into smaller date ranges

---

## Common mistakes

> **Pitfalls met when writing code against auditor 5.x, and the correct form**

### Looking for the Doctrine provider in the core

Since auditor 5.0, `damienharper/auditor` contains no Doctrine code. `DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\…`
classes come from `damienharper/auditor-doctrine-provider`; Symfony applications install
`damienharper/auditor-bundle`, which requires it. See [Which packages do I need?](getting-started/which-packages.md).

### Mixing major versions

`auditor-bundle` 8.x goes with auditor 5.x and `auditor-doctrine-provider` 2.x; `auditor-bundle` 7.x
with auditor 4.x and `auditor-doctrine-provider` 1.x. Code written for one line does not run on the
other: the audit table format and several entry fields changed in 5.0 ([upgrade guide](upgrade/v5.md)).

### Decoding `extraData` twice

```php
// ❌ $entry->extraData is already an array (or null)
$data = json_decode($entry->extraData, true);

// ✅
$data = $entry->extraData ?? [];
```

The same holds for `$entry->blame`, already decoded, and `getDiffs()`, which returns an array.

### Reading an `action` key from a `LifecycleEvent`

The payload of a `LifecycleEvent` carries the operation in `type`, as a string:

```php
// ❌ there is no 'action' key
$operation = $event->getPayload()['action'];

// ✅
$operation = $event->getPayload()['type']; // 'insert', 'update', 'remove', 'associate', 'dissociate'
```

### Comparing `Entry::$type` with an enum case

`$entry->type` is a plain string. Compare it with the enum value or the string constant:

```php
use DH\Auditor\Model\TransactionType;

// ❌ always false: a string is never identical to an enum case
$entry->type === TransactionType::Update;

// ✅
$entry->type === TransactionType::Update->value;
$entry->type === TransactionType::UPDATE;
```

### Using fields removed in 5.0

| Removed (4.x and earlier)                         | Use instead (5.x)                                              |
|---------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------|
| `$entry->transactionHash`                         | `$entry->transactionId` (a ULID)                               |
| payload keys `blame_user`, `blame_user_fqdn`, `blame_user_firewall`, `ip` | payload key `blame` (JSON: `username`, `user_fqdn`, `user_firewall`, `ip`) |
| `DH\Auditor\Transaction\NeedsConversionToAuditableType` | `DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Transaction\NeedsConversionToAuditableType` (in `auditor-doctrine-provider`) |
| `DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Auditing\Attribute\{Auditable,Ignore,Security}` (deprecated 4.x aliases) | `DH\Auditor\Attribute\{Auditable,Ignore,Security}` |

### Expecting DQL or raw SQL to be audited

The Doctrine provider audits the changes flushed through the Doctrine ORM unit of work. Bulk DQL
`UPDATE`/`DELETE` queries and raw SQL statements bypass it and are not recorded.

### Hiding a secret with `#[Ignore]`, or leaking a masked one

`#[Ignore]` drops the field from the audit: its changes are not recorded at all. To record that a sensitive field
changed without storing its values, use `#[Mask]` (`"***"`, or an HMAC with `MaskStrategy::KeyedHash`, which needs the
provider's mask secret). Only the values in the diffs are masked: the label of the entity (its `__toString()` or a
label resolver) is stored in clear in every entry, so never build it from a masked field.

### Using DoctrineAuditBundle names

`dh_doctrine_audit`, `DH\DoctrineAuditBundle\…` and annotations such as
`DH\DoctrineAuditBundle\Annotation\Auditable` belong to the former DoctrineAuditBundle. See
[Coming from DoctrineAuditBundle](getting-started/coming-from-doctrine-audit-bundle.md).

---

## Blame Context

> **Record how a change was made, not only who made it**

The [user provider](user-provider.md) tells *who* made a change. A blame context tells *how*: an import,
a console command, a Messenger message, an API token, a cron job… It is written in the `via` key of the
`blame` JSON of every audit entry, next to the user.

```json
{
  "username": "alice",
  "user_fqdn": "App\\Entity\\User",
  "user_firewall": "main",
  "ip": "10.0.0.1",
  "via": { "type": "import", "label": "Import batch #42", "data": { "file": "products.csv" } }
}
```

No schema change is needed: `via` is one more key of the `blame` JSON column (schema v2).

### 🧩 The blame context

```php
use DH\Auditor\Blame\BlameContext;

new BlameContext(
    type: 'import',                    // required: kind of context
    label: 'Import batch #42',         // optional: human readable label
    data: ['file' => 'products.csv'],  // optional: JSON encodable data
    user: null,                        // optional: user to blame instead of the user provider's one
);
```

| Property | Written in `via` | Purpose |
|----------|------------------|---------|
| `type`   | ✅ always         | Kind of context, such as `import`, `console`, `messenger`, `api_token` |
| `label`  | ✅ when set       | What the viewer shows next to the type |
| `data`   | ✅ when not empty | Anything else worth keeping |
| `user`   | ❌                | Blamed instead of the user returned by the user provider (`blame_id`, `username`, `user_fqdn`, `impersonator`) |

The `user` lets a background process blame the person it acts for, such as the user who dispatched a message,
instead of the process itself. The IP address and firewall still come from the security provider.

### 📚 The blame context stack

Contexts are pushed on a stack held by the auditor configuration; the audit entries get the **current** one
(the last pushed). Nested contexts are not chained: only the innermost is written.

```php
$stack = $auditor->getConfiguration()->getBlameContextStack();

$stack->run(new BlameContext('import', 'Import batch #42'), function () use ($entityManager): void {
    // ... create or update entities ...
    $entityManager->flush();
});
```

| Method | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `run(BlameContext $context, callable $callback): mixed` | Pushes the context, runs the callback and pops the context, even if the callback throws |
| `push(BlameContext $context): void` | Pushes a context |
| `pop(): ?BlameContext` | Pops the current context |
| `current(): ?BlameContext` | Returns the current context, or `null` |
| `isEmpty(): bool` | Whether no context is set |
| `reset(): void` | Empties the stack |

> [!TIP]
> Prefer `run()`: a context pushed and never popped (because of an exception) would be written in the audit
> entries of every following flush. In long-running processes (Messenger workers, FrankenPHP or RoadRunner
> workers), call `reset()` between two units of work. `auditor-bundle` does it for you.

The context is captured **when the entities are flushed**, not when the audit entries are written: a context
popped before the database transaction is committed still applies to the flushes made while it was current.

### 📖 Reading it back

```php
$entry->via;               // ['type' => 'import', 'label' => 'Import batch #42', 'data' => [...]] or null
$entry->blame['via'];      // same value, from the decoded blame
$entry->toArray()['blame_via']; // exports
```

Entries written without a blame context have no `via` key (`$entry->via` is `null`).

---

## Configuration Reference

> **All configuration options available in auditor**

This section covers all configuration options available in auditor.

### ⚙️ Auditor Configuration

The main `Configuration` class accepts the following options:

```php
<?php

use DH\Auditor\Configuration;

$configuration = new Configuration([
    'enabled' => true,
    'timezone' => 'UTC',
    'user_provider' => null,
    'security_provider' => null,
    'role_checker' => null,
    'extra_data_provider' => null,
]);
```

#### Options Reference

| Option              | Type              | Default | Description                                         |
|---------------------|-------------------|---------|-----------------------------------------------------|
| `enabled`           | `bool`            | `true`  | Enable or disable auditing globally                 |
| `timezone`          | `string`          | `'UTC'` | Timezone used for audit timestamps                  |
| `user_provider`     | `callable\|null`  | `null`  | Callback that returns the current user              |
| `security_provider` | `callable\|null`  | `null`  | Callback that returns security context info         |
| `role_checker`      | `callable\|null`  | `null`  | Callback that checks if user can view entity audits |
| `extra_data_provider` | `callable\|null` | `null` | Callback that returns the `extra_data` of the entries of a flush (see [Extra Data](../extra-data.md)) |

### 🔧 Configuration Methods

#### Enable/Disable Auditing

```php
// Disable auditing
$configuration->disable();

// Re-enable auditing
$configuration->enable();

// Check if auditing is enabled
if ($configuration->enabled) {
    // ...
}
```

#### Get Timezone

```php
$timezone = $configuration->timezone;
```

### 👤 User Provider

The user provider is a callable that returns information about the current user. This is used to record who made each change.

```php
use DH\Auditor\User\User;

$configuration->setUserProvider(function (): ?User {
    // Return null if no user is authenticated
    $currentUser = $this->security->getUser();
    
    if (null === $currentUser) {
        return null;
    }
    
    return new User(
        (string) $currentUser->getId(),  // User identifier
        $currentUser->getUsername(),      // Username for display
        $currentUser::class,              // Class of the user (user_fqdn)
    );
});
```

The `User` class implements `UserInterface`:

```php
namespace DH\Auditor\User;

interface UserInterface
{
    public ?string $identifier { get; }
    public ?string $username { get; }
    public ?string $fqdn { get; }
    public ?UserInterface $impersonator { get; }
}
```

See [User Provider Configuration](user-provider.md) for more details. To record *how* a change was made (an
import, a command, a message…), see [Blame Context](blame-context.md).

### 🔐 Security Provider

The security provider returns the client IP address and the firewall name, as a list of two values:

```php
$configuration->setSecurityProvider(function (): array {
    return [
        $_SERVER['REMOTE_ADDR'] ?? null, // client IP
        $this->getFirewallName(),        // firewall name
    ];
});
```

See [Security Provider Configuration](security-provider.md) for more details.

### 🛡️ Role Checker

The role checker determines whether a user can view audits for a specific entity:

```php
$configuration->setRoleChecker(function (string $entity, string $scope): bool {
    // $entity is the FQCN of the audited entity
    // $scope is the action (e.g., 'view')
    
    // Example: Only admins can view User audits
    if ($entity === User::class) {
        return $this->security->isGranted('ROLE_ADMIN');
    }
    
    // Allow everyone to view other audits
    return true;
});
```

See [Role Checker Configuration](role-checker.md) for more details.

### 🗄️ DoctrineProvider Configuration

The DoctrineProvider has its own configuration. See [DoctrineProvider Configuration](https://damienharper.github.io/auditor-docs/auditor-doctrine-provider/providers/doctrine/configuration) for details.

### 📝 Configuration Summary

```php
<?php

use DH\Auditor\Auditor;
use DH\Auditor\Configuration;
use DH\Auditor\User\User;
use Symfony\Component\EventDispatcher\EventDispatcher;

$configuration = new Configuration([
    'enabled' => true,
    'timezone' => 'Europe/Paris',
]);

// Set user provider
$configuration->setUserProvider(function (): ?User {
    $user = $securityContext->getUser();
    if (null === $user) {
        return null;
    }
    return new User((string) $user->getId(), $user->getUsername(), $user::class);
});

// Set security provider
$configuration->setSecurityProvider(function (): array {
    return [$_SERVER['REMOTE_ADDR'] ?? null, null];
});

// Set role checker
$configuration->setRoleChecker(function (string $entity, string $scope): bool {
    return $this->authorizationChecker->isGranted('ROLE_AUDIT_VIEWER');
});

$auditor = new Auditor($configuration, new EventDispatcher());
```

- 🧭 [Blame Context](blame-context.md)

## Role Checker Configuration

> **Control access to audit logs with fine-grained permissions**

The role checker controls access to audit logs, allowing you to restrict who can view audits for specific entities.

### 🔍 Overview

The role checker is a callback that is invoked when someone attempts to read audit entries. It determines whether the current user has permission to view the requested audits.

> [!WARNING]
> If access is denied, an `AccessDeniedException` is thrown.

### 🚀 Setting Up a Role Checker

#### Basic Example

```php
<?php

use DH\Auditor\Configuration;

$configuration = new Configuration(['enabled' => true]);

$configuration->setRoleChecker(function (string $entity, string $scope): bool {
    // $entity - The fully qualified class name of the entity being audited
    // $scope  - The action being performed (e.g., 'view')
    
    // Return true to allow access, false to deny
    return true;
});
```

#### Symfony Security Integration

```php
<?php

use App\Entity\User;
use App\Entity\Payment;
use Symfony\Bundle\SecurityBundle\Security;

$configuration->setRoleChecker(function (string $entity, string $scope) use ($security): bool {
    // Admins can view all audits
    if ($security->isGranted('ROLE_ADMIN')) {
        return true;
    }
    
    // Managers can view most audits
    if ($security->isGranted('ROLE_MANAGER')) {
        // But not User audits (sensitive)
        return $entity !== User::class;
    }
    
    // Accountants can only view Payment audits
    if ($security->isGranted('ROLE_ACCOUNTANT')) {
        return $entity === Payment::class;
    }
    
    // Deny all other users
    return false;
});
```

### 📋 Parameters

The role checker receives two parameters:

| Parameter | Type     | Description                                      |
|-----------|----------|--------------------------------------------------|
| `$entity` | `string` | The FQCN of the entity being queried             |
| `$scope`  | `string` | The action scope (currently only `'view'`)       |

#### Available Scopes

| Scope  | Constant                     | Description                |
|--------|------------------------------|----------------------------|
| `view` | `Security::VIEW_SCOPE`       | Viewing audit entries      |

### 🏷️ Using Entity-Level Security Attributes

You can also define view permissions directly on entities using the `#[Security]` attribute:

```php
<?php

use DH\Auditor\Attribute\Auditable;
use DH\Auditor\Attribute\Security;
use Doctrine\ORM\Mapping as ORM;

#[ORM\Entity]
#[Auditable]
#[Security(view: ['ROLE_ADMIN', 'ROLE_AUDIT_VIEWER'])]
class SensitiveEntity
{
    // ...
}
```

The role checker should then verify these roles:

```php
<?php

$configuration->setRoleChecker(function (string $entity, string $scope) use ($security, $provider): bool {
    // Get entity configuration (including security roles from attributes)
    $configuration = $provider->getConfiguration();
    $entities = $configuration->getEntities();
    
    if (!isset($entities[$entity]['roles'][$scope])) {
        // No specific roles defined, allow access
        return true;
    }
    
    $requiredRoles = $entities[$entity]['roles'][$scope];
    
    // Check if user has any of the required roles
    foreach ($requiredRoles as $role) {
        if ($security->isGranted($role)) {
            return true;
        }
    }
    
    return false;
});
```

### 🧩 Complex Authorization Logic

#### Per-Entity Custom Rules

```php
<?php

$configuration->setRoleChecker(function (string $entity, string $scope) use ($security, $em): bool {
    $user = $security->getUser();
    
    if (null === $user) {
        return false;
    }
    
    // Check ownership-based access for certain entities
    switch ($entity) {
        case Order::class:
            // Users can view their own orders' audits
            // Admins can view all
            if ($security->isGranted('ROLE_ADMIN')) {
                return true;
            }
            
            // This would need additional context about which order is being queried
            return $security->isGranted('ROLE_ORDER_AUDITOR');
            
        case User::class:
            // Only super admins can view user audits
            return $security->isGranted('ROLE_SUPER_ADMIN');
            
        default:
            // Default: allow managers and above
            return $security->isGranted('ROLE_MANAGER');
    }
});
```

#### Time-Based Restrictions

```php
<?php

$configuration->setRoleChecker(function (string $entity, string $scope) use ($security): bool {
    // Only allow audit viewing during business hours for non-admins
    if (!$security->isGranted('ROLE_ADMIN')) {
        $hour = (int) date('H');
        if ($hour < 9 || $hour > 17) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    
    return $security->isGranted('ROLE_AUDITOR');
});
```

### ⚠️ Error Handling

When the role checker returns `false`, an `AccessDeniedException` is thrown:

```php
<?php

use DH\Auditor\Exception\AccessDeniedException;
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Reader; // from auditor-doctrine-provider

$reader = new Reader($provider);

try {
    $query = $reader->createQuery(SensitiveEntity::class);
    $audits = $query->execute();
} catch (AccessDeniedException $e) {
    // Handle access denied
    // $e->getMessage() contains details about the denial
}
```

### 🚫 No Role Checker

> [!CAUTION]
> If no role checker is configured (`null`), all users have access to all audit logs. This is not recommended for production environments.

```php
// This allows everyone to view all audits
$configuration = new Configuration([
    'role_checker' => null,  // No access control
]);
```

### ✅ Best Practices

1. **Always implement a role checker in production** - Don't leave audits open to everyone
2. **Log access attempts** - Consider logging who accesses audit data
3. **Use the principle of least privilege** - Only grant access where necessary
4. **Consider data sensitivity** - Some entities may contain sensitive information
5. **Test your rules** - Ensure your authorization logic works as expected

---

### Related

- 🏷️ [Security Attribute](https://damienharper.github.io/auditor-docs/auditor-doctrine-provider/providers/doctrine/attributes#-security)
- 👤 [User Provider Configuration](user-provider.md)
- 🔐 [Security Provider Configuration](security-provider.md)

## Security Provider Configuration

> **Capture contextual security information for each audit event**

The security provider captures additional contextual information about each audit event: the client IP address and
the firewall name.

### 🔍 Overview

When an audit entry is created, the security provider supplies:

- **the client IP address**, stored under the `ip` key of the `blame` JSON column;
- **the firewall name**, stored under the `user_firewall` key of the `blame` JSON column.

The class of the user (`user_fqdn`) is not supplied by the security provider: it is the `fqdn` of the user returned by
the [user provider](user-provider.md).

### 🚀 Setting Up a Security Provider

The security provider is a callable (or a `DH\Auditor\Security\SecurityProviderInterface` implementation) that
returns a **list of two values**: the client IP address, then the firewall name. Either may be `null`.

#### Basic Example

```php
<?php

use DH\Auditor\Configuration;

$configuration = new Configuration(['enabled' => true]);

$configuration->setSecurityProvider(function (): array {
    return [
        $_SERVER['REMOTE_ADDR'] ?? null, // client IP
        null,                            // firewall
    ];
});
```

#### Complete Symfony Example

```php
<?php

use DH\Auditor\Security\SecurityProviderInterface;
use Symfony\Bundle\SecurityBundle\Security\FirewallMap;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\RequestStack;

final readonly class SecurityProvider implements SecurityProviderInterface
{
    public function __construct(
        private RequestStack $requestStack,
        private FirewallMap $firewallMap,
    ) {}

    public function __invoke(): array
    {
        $request = $this->requestStack->getCurrentRequest();
        if (null === $request) {
            return [null, null];
        }

        return [
            $request->getClientIp(),
            $this->firewallMap->getFirewallConfig($request)?->getName(),
        ];
    }
}

$configuration->setSecurityProvider($securityProvider);
```

> [!NOTE]
> auditor-bundle ships such a security provider and configures it for you.

### 📋 Return Value Structure

The security provider must return a list (positional array) of two values:

| Position | Type           | Description                                     |
|----------|----------------|-------------------------------------------------|
| `0`      | `string\|null` | The IP address of the client making the request |
| `1`      | `string\|null` | The name of the security firewall used          |

> [!WARNING]
> Return a list, not an associative array: the values are read by position, so keys such as `client_ip` are not
> recognized and the IP address and firewall are stored as `null`.

### 🌐 Handling Different Contexts

#### Behind a Proxy

> [!TIP]
> When behind a load balancer or reverse proxy, ensure trusted proxies are configured in Symfony. The
> `getClientIp()` method then handles `X-Forwarded-For` automatically.

#### CLI Commands and Workers

There is no request in a console command or a Messenger worker: return `[null, null]`, or a value of your choice:

```php
$configuration->setSecurityProvider(function () use ($requestStack): array {
    $request = $requestStack->getCurrentRequest();

    if (null === $request) {
        return [null, null];      // console command, worker…
    }

    return [$request->getClientIp(), str_starts_with($request->getPathInfo(), '/api') ? 'api' : 'main'];
});
```

To record *how* a change was made outside a web request (a command, an import, a message), use a
[blame context](blame-context.md) rather than a fake IP address or firewall.

### 🔍 Accessing Security Info from Audit Entries

When reading audit entries:

```php
<?php

$reader = new Reader($provider);
$audits = $reader->createQuery(Post::class)->execute();

foreach ($audits as $entry) {
    echo "IP Address: " . $entry->ip;
    echo "User Class: " . $entry->userFqdn;
    echo "Firewall: " . $entry->userFirewall;
}
```

### 🌐 IP Address Format

The IP address is stored as a string in the `blame` JSON column, IPv4 (`192.168.1.1`) or IPv6
(`2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334`).

### ✅ Best Practices

1. **Always handle a null request** - The request may not be available (CLI, async jobs)
2. **Configure trusted proxies** - When behind a reverse proxy
3. **Always return two values** - `[$ip, $firewall]`, each possibly `null`
4. **Consider privacy regulations** - IP logging may be subject to GDPR or similar laws

> [!NOTE]
> Remember to comply with privacy regulations when storing IP addresses. Consider implementing data retention policies.

---

### Related

- 👤 [User Provider Configuration](user-provider.md)
- 🛡️ [Role Checker Configuration](role-checker.md)
- 🧭 [Blame Context](blame-context.md)

## User Provider Configuration

> **Identify who made changes to audited entities**

The user provider is responsible for identifying who made changes to audited entities.

### 🔍 Overview

When an audit entry is created, auditor can record:

- **blame_id** - The unique identifier of the user
- **username** - The username or display name (stored in the `blame` JSON column)

This information comes from the user provider callback.

### 🚀 Setting Up a User Provider

#### Basic Example

```php
<?php

use DH\Auditor\Configuration;
use DH\Auditor\User\User;

$configuration = new Configuration([
    'enabled' => true,
]);

$configuration->setUserProvider(function (): ?User {
    // Get the currently authenticated user from your application
    $currentUser = $this->getAuthenticatedUser();
    
    if (null === $currentUser) {
        return null;  // No user authenticated
    }
    
    return new User(
        (string) $currentUser->getId(),    // User ID (stored as blame_id)
        $currentUser->getUsername(),        // Username (stored in blame JSON column)
        $currentUser::class,                // Class of the user (user_fqdn key of the blame JSON column)
    );
});
```

#### Symfony Security Integration

```php
<?php

use DH\Auditor\User\User;
use Symfony\Bundle\SecurityBundle\Security;

// In a service or controller
$configuration->setUserProvider(function () use ($security): ?User {
    $user = $security->getUser();
    
    if (null === $user) {
        return null;
    }
    
    return new User(
        $user->getUserIdentifier(),
        $user->getUserIdentifier(),
        $user::class,
    );
});
```

#### With User Entity ID

If your user has a database ID:

```php
<?php

use App\Entity\User as AppUser;
use DH\Auditor\User\User;

$configuration->setUserProvider(function () use ($security, $entityManager): ?User {
    $user = $security->getUser();
    
    if (null === $user) {
        return null;
    }
    
    // Get the user ID from the database entity
    $userId = $entityManager
        ->getRepository(AppUser::class)
        ->findOneBy(['email' => $user->getUserIdentifier()])
        ?->getId();
    
    return new User(
        (string) ($userId ?? $user->getUserIdentifier()),
        $user->getUserIdentifier()
    );
});
```

### 📦 The User Class

The built-in `User` class is a final value object. `UserInterface` declares four read-only properties (PHP 8.4
property hooks), read by the providers:

```php
<?php

namespace DH\Auditor\User;

interface UserInterface
{
    public ?string $identifier { get; }   // stored as blame_id

    public ?string $username { get; }     // stored in the blame JSON column

    public ?string $fqdn { get; }         // class of the user, user_fqdn key of the blame JSON column

    public ?UserInterface $impersonator { get; } // impersonator key of the blame JSON column
}

final class User implements UserInterface
{
    public ?string $identifier {
        get => $this->id;
    }

    public function __construct(
        private readonly ?string $id = null,
        public readonly ?string $username = null,
        public readonly ?string $fqdn = null,
        public readonly ?UserInterface $impersonator = null,
    ) {}
}
```

`fqdn` is the class of the user in your application (such as `App\Entity\User`), recorded as `user_fqdn`: it tells
users of different classes apart when they share an id. It is null when the user provider does not supply it.

### 🎭 Impersonation

When a user impersonates another one (switch user), return the impersonated user and pass the impersonator: the
changes are blamed on the impersonated user, and the impersonator is recorded in the `impersonator` key of the
blame JSON column.

```php
<?php

return new User(
    (string) $impersonated->getId(),
    $impersonated->getUserIdentifier(),
    $impersonated::class,
    new User((string) $impersonator->getId(), $impersonator->getUserIdentifier(), $impersonator::class),
);
```

```json
{
  "username": "alice",
  "user_fqdn": "App\\Entity\\Customer",
  "user_firewall": "main",
  "ip": "10.0.0.1",
  "impersonator": {"id": "1", "username": "admin", "fqdn": "App\\Entity\\Admin"}
}
```

The key is written only when an impersonator is set; `$entry->impersonator` returns it (null otherwise).

### 🧩 Custom User Implementation

You can create your own user class by implementing `UserInterface`:

```php
<?php

namespace App\Audit;

use DH\Auditor\User\UserInterface;

final readonly class CustomUser implements UserInterface
{
    public ?string $identifier;
    public ?string $username;
    public ?string $fqdn;
    public ?UserInterface $impersonator;

    public function __construct(string $id, string $name, public string $email)
    {
        $this->identifier = $id;
        $this->username = sprintf('%s (%s)', $name, $email);
        $this->fqdn = \App\Entity\User::class;
        $this->impersonator = null;
    }
}
```

A readonly property satisfies a `{ get; }` property of an interface.

### 🌐 API/CLI Context

> [!TIP]
> For API requests, consider identifying the API client rather than leaving the user empty. For CLI commands,
> return `null` (no fake user) and record how the change was made with a [blame context](blame-context.md),
> such as `new BlameContext('console', 'app:import-products')`.

```php
<?php

$configuration->setUserProvider(function (): ?User {
    // CLI context: no user to blame, the command is recorded by a blame context
    if (PHP_SAPI === 'cli') {
        return null;
    }
    
    // Check for API token
    $apiToken = $_SERVER['HTTP_X_API_TOKEN'] ?? null;
    if ($apiToken) {
        $apiUser = $this->apiUserRepository->findByToken($apiToken);
        if ($apiUser) {
            return new User(
                (string) $apiUser->getId(),
                sprintf('API: %s', $apiUser->getName())
            );
        }
    }
    
    // Regular web user
    $user = $this->security->getUser();
    if ($user) {
        return new User(
            $user->getUserIdentifier(),
            $user->getUserIdentifier()
        );
    }
    
    return null;
});
```

### 🔍 Accessing User Info from Audit Entries

When reading audit entries, you can access the recorded user information:

```php
<?php

$reader = new Reader($provider);
$query = $reader->createQuery(Post::class, ['object_id' => 123]);
$audits = $query->execute();

foreach ($audits as $entry) {
    echo "User ID: " . $entry->userId;    // blame_id column
    echo "Username: " . $entry->username; // blame JSON → username key
    echo "User FQDN: " . $entry->userFqdn; // blame JSON → user_fqdn key
    echo "Impersonator: " . ($entry->impersonator['username'] ?? '-'); // blame JSON → impersonator key
}
```

### ✅ Best Practices

1. **Always return `null` when no user is available** - Don't create fake users
2. **Use meaningful identifiers** - Use the actual user ID, not just the username
3. **Include useful context in the username** - Consider including role or context info
4. **Handle all authentication methods** - Consider API tokens, CLI, impersonation, etc.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Always return `null` when there's no authenticated user. Don't create placeholder users as this can lead to confusing audit trails.
