### 🧪 Flush benchmarks

#### Method

The benchmark is `benchmarks/AuditBench.php` ([PHPBench](https://phpbench.readthedocs.io/)). Each scenario changes
`N` entities of the test fixtures (`Author`, `Post`, `Tag`), all audited, and measures the single `flush()` that
writes them — the Doctrine work and the auditing (changesets, diffs, audit rows). The schema is rebuilt and the data
seeded before each iteration, outside the measured time.

| Scenario     | Measured flush                                                                    | Audit rows |
|--------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------:|
| `insert`     | insert `N` authors                                                                | `N`        |
| `update`     | update 3 fields of `N` posts                                                      | `N`        |
| `remove`     | remove `N` authors                                                                | `N`        |
| `associate`  | add a tag to `N` posts (many-to-many)                                             | `2N`       |
| `dissociate` | remove that tag from `N` posts                                                    | `2N`       |
| `mixed`      | insert `N/2` authors, update `N/4` of the existing ones (2 fields), remove `N/4`  | `N`        |

Three configurations were measured back to back, for each database and each `N`:

| Configuration                | Code                                                                       |
|------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 1.2.1                        | tag `1.2.1` (latest 1.x release), schema v1                                |
| 2.0-dev, `batch_size: 0`     | `main` at `169793e` (batch INSERT), schema v2, one `INSERT` per entry¹ |
| 2.0-dev, `batch_size: 500`   | the same code with `batch_size: 500`                                       |

¹ The PostgreSQL `N` = 50 triplet was run again on `main` at `ae51e10`, which only changes `audit:schema:migrate`
(see [Reading the results](#reading-the-results)). The first MySQL `N` = 1,000 triplet was discarded and run again:
a dependency installation was running on the machine at the same time.

1.2.1 has no benchmark: `benchmarks/AuditBench.php` and `phpbench.json` of `main` were copied into a checkout of the
`1.2.1` tag, with one change — the `batch_size` option was removed from the provider configuration, since 1.2.1 does
not have it (its configuration rejects unknown options). The scenarios, fixtures and data are the same.

Settings: `N` = 50, 500 and 1,000; 10 iterations of 1 revolution, no warm-up; the reported value is the **mode** of
the 10 iterations (PHPBench's kernel density estimate), with its relative standard deviation (rstdev).

#### Environment

| Item       | Value                                                                                         |
|------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Machine    | Apple M3 (8 cores), 16 GiB RAM, macOS 27.3                                                    |
| PHP        | 8.5.12 (CLI, NTS), Xdebug not loaded and `XDEBUG_MODE=off`, OPcache disabled for the CLI      |
| Libraries  | doctrine/dbal 4.6.0, doctrine/orm 3.8.0, phpbench 1.7.0; damienharper/auditor 4.3.1 (1.2.1) and `master` at `aca4003` (2.0-dev) |
| SQLite     | file database on the local SSD (`pdo-sqlite`)                                                 |
| MySQL      | 8.0.46 (`mysql:8.0` image, default configuration), `pdo-mysql`                                |
| PostgreSQL | 15.20 (`postgres:15` image, default configuration), `pdo-pgsql`                               |
| Containers | OrbStack (8 CPUs, 9.8 GiB), data on Docker volumes (on disk, no tmpfs), reached on `127.0.0.1` |

#### Reproduce

Start the databases (any MySQL 8 / PostgreSQL 15 server will do; the benchmark empties the database it is given):

```bash
docker run -d --name bench-mysql -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=password -e MYSQL_DATABASE=bench -e MYSQL_USER=auditor -e MYSQL_PASSWORD=password -p 33377:3306 mysql:8.0
```

```bash
docker run -d --name bench-pgsql -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=password -e POSTGRES_DB=bench -p 54377:5432 postgres:15
```

Run a configuration (here 2.0 with `batch_size: 500`, 1,000 entities, PostgreSQL):

```bash
BENCH_N=1000 BENCH_BATCH_SIZE=500 BENCH_DATABASE_URL='pdo-pgsql://postgres:password@127.0.0.1:54377/bench?serverVersion=15' XDEBUG_MODE=off vendor/bin/phpbench run benchmarks/AuditBench.php --iterations=10 --revs=1 --report=aggregate
```

- `BENCH_DATABASE_URL` takes a DBAL URL. Use the `pdo-mysql://`, `pdo-pgsql://` and `pdo-sqlite:///` schemes: with
  `pgsql://`, DBAL picks the native `pgsql` driver. For SQLite on disk, give an absolute path after the third slash
  (`pdo-sqlite:////path/to/bench.sqlite`); without `BENCH_DATABASE_URL`, the benchmark uses in-memory SQLite.
- `BENCH_BATCH_SIZE` defaults to `0`; it is ignored by the 1.2.1 copy of the benchmark.
- Run the configurations you compare back to back, with the same `N`, and nothing else running on the machine.

#### Results

Mode in milliseconds, rstdev in parentheses, and change against 1.2.1 (negative = faster).

#### Reading the results

- **Dispersion.** On SQLite and PostgreSQL, most rstdev values stay below 5 %: differences above 5 % are
  meaningful. MySQL (through the container's virtualized disk) is much noisier, with rstdev up to 51 %: there, only
  the large gains of `batch_size: 500` are significant, and the ±20 % differences between 1.2.1 and
  `batch_size: 0` are not. At `N` = 50, a flush lasts a few dozen milliseconds and the rstdev reaches 10 to 25 % on
  PostgreSQL too: the first run of the PostgreSQL `N` = 50 triplet gave the `insert` scenario 27.8 ms with 1.2.1 and
  47.2 ms with `batch_size: 0` (+70 %); run again, the three configurations back to back, it gave 43.3 ms and
  38.1 ms (−12 %). The second run is the one reported above: at `N` = 50, read only the large differences.
- **`batch_size: 0`.** Each audit entry is written with its own `INSERT`, as in 1.2.1: the schema v2 changes (JSON
  `blame`, ULID `transaction_id`, diffs envelope) do not make a flush measurably slower.
- **`batch_size: 500`.** The gain grows with `N` and with the cost of a round trip: modest on SQLite (no network,
  10 to 18 %), large on PostgreSQL (half of the time or less from `N` = 500). `associate` and `dissociate`, which write
  two audit rows per changed entity, gain the most. With `N` = 50, a flush writes 50 to 100 rows, a single multi-row
  statement: the gain is already visible but within a noisier range.

### 🗄️ Schema v2 migration

The migration of a schema v1 audit table (see [Upgrading to 2.0](../../upgrade/v2.md)) was timed on a table of
**1,000,000 rows** written by 1.2.1, with `audit:schema:migrate --force --convert-all` (2.0-dev, `main` at
`e081182`), on the machine and database servers described above.

#### Method

- **Data**: `author_audit`, generated with 1.2.1 (not measured) by cycles of three flushes, each in its own
  transaction: insert 20 authors, update them (2 fields), remove 10 of them. That is 50 audit rows and 3 transactions
  per cycle, i.e. **60,000 transactions** for 1,000,000 rows (547 MiB on MySQL, 447 MiB on PostgreSQL).
- **Run**: one database after the other, nothing else running; the command output is timestamped to get the duration
  of each step.

#### Results

| Step                                                  | MySQL 8.0         | PostgreSQL 15     |
|-------------------------------------------------------|------------------:|------------------:|
| Additive DDL (new columns, `schema_version`, `blame`) | 50 s              | 43 s              |
| `transaction_hash` → `transaction_id` (60,000 ULIDs)  | 100 s             | 29 s              |
| Diffs conversion (1,000,000 rows)                     | 139 s             | 118 s             |
| Legacy columns dropped                                | < 1 s             | < 1 s             |
| **Total**                                             | **4 min 59 s**    | **3 min 13 s**    |
| Table size after `OPTIMIZE TABLE` / `VACUUM FULL`     | 690 MiB (+26 %)   | 614 MiB (+37 %)   |

After the migration, both tables had 60,000 distinct `transaction_id` values (one per legacy transaction, the
grouping is kept), no row without `transaction_id`, `blame` or `source` in its diffs, and every row at
`schema_version` 2.

- **What takes the time**: every row is read, its diffs decoded, rewritten in the v2 envelope and updated. Both
  conversions work in batches of 500 rows (or transactions), each written in one database transaction, and read the
  rows through the primary key or the `transaction_hash` index: their duration grows linearly with the size of the
  audit tables.
- **Disk space**: the rows are rewritten in place, so the table grows during the migration (878 MiB on MySQL and up
  to 1,783 MiB on PostgreSQL right after it, dead rows included) until InnoDB or autovacuum reuses the space, or
  until an `OPTIMIZE TABLE` / `VACUUM FULL` reclaims it. On PostgreSQL, the table reached up to 4 times its initial
  size: check the free disk space before migrating.
- **Your own estimate**: `--limit=N` converts only `N` transactions or rows and keeps the legacy columns, so that a
  later run resumes where it stopped. Time a run on a sample and extrapolate linearly; test on a copy of your
  production data, with a backup, before the real migration.

#### Reproduce

The scripts are not part of the repository; the steps are:

1. With a checkout of the `1.2.1` tag, create the audit schema and write the v1 audit rows (any audited entity and
   workload will do; the larger the table, the more representative the figures).
2. With 2.0, register the same entities and run the command, timing it:

```bash
time bin/console audit:schema:migrate --force --convert-all
```

### Next Steps

- ⚙️ [Configuration](configuration.md) — `batch_size` and the other options
- 🚀 [Upgrading to 2.0](../../upgrade/v2.md) — migrating the audit tables

## Schema Management

> **Create and manage audit tables in your database**

This guide covers how to create and manage audit tables using the `SchemaManager`.

### 🔍 Overview

For each audited entity, the provider creates a corresponding audit table to store the change history. The `SchemaManager` class handles all schema operations using DBAL's schema introspection API.

The schema can be managed in two ways:

1. **Automatically** — via Doctrine's `postGenerateSchemaTable` event (integrates with `doctrine:schema:update` / Migrations)
2. **Manually** — by calling `SchemaManager::updateAuditSchema()` directly

### 🏗️ Audit Table Structure (schema version 2)

Each audit table created by the current provider has the following structure:

```sql
CREATE TABLE posts_audit (
    id               BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    schema_version   SMALLINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL DEFAULT 2,
    type             VARCHAR(11)  NOT NULL,
    object_id        VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    discriminator    VARCHAR(255) NULL,
    transaction_id   CHAR(26)     NULL,
    diffs            JSON         NULL,
    extra_data       JSON         NULL,
    blame_id         VARCHAR(255) NULL,
    blame            JSON         NULL,
    created_at       DATETIME     NOT NULL,

    INDEX type_idx            (type),
    INDEX object_id_type_idx  (object_id, type),
    INDEX transaction_id_idx  (transaction_id),
    INDEX blame_id_created_at_idx (blame_id, created_at),
    INDEX created_at_idx      (created_at)
);
```

The SQL is illustrative: the actual index names are generated from a hash of the table name
(`type_<md5>_idx`…), and the column types depend on the platform (JSON on MySQL / MariaDB, JSONB on PostgreSQL,
TEXT on SQLite).

#### Column Details

| Column           | Type                | Description                                                       |
|------------------|---------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `id`             | BIGINT (PK)         | Auto-increment primary key                                        |
| `schema_version` | SMALLINT            | Diffs format version: `1` (legacy) or `2` (current)              |
| `type`           | VARCHAR(11)         | Action: insert, update, remove, associate, dissociate             |
| `object_id`      | VARCHAR(255)        | The primary key of the audited entity                             |
| `discriminator`  | VARCHAR(255)        | Entity class (used in inheritance hierarchies)                    |
| `transaction_id` | CHAR(26)            | ULID grouping changes from the same flush batch                   |
| `diffs`          | JSON                | JSON-encoded change data (see format below)                       |
| `extra_data`     | JSON                | Custom extra data (populated via `LifecycleEvent` listener)       |
| `blame_id`       | VARCHAR(255)        | User identifier who made the change                               |
| `blame`          | JSON                | Blame: `username`, `user_fqdn`, `user_firewall`, `ip`, `impersonator` when the user is impersonated, and `via` when a blame context is set |
| `created_at`     | DATETIME            | When the audit entry was created                                  |

#### Diffs Format (schema version 2)

All entry types share a unified JSON envelope:

```json
{
    "source":  { "id": "42", "class": "App\\Entity\\Post", "label": "Hello World", "table": "posts" },
    "changes": {
        "title":   { "old": "Hello World", "new": "Hello auditor!" },
        "content": { "old": null,           "new": "My first post." }
    }
}
```

- `source` — always present: entity id, FQCN, label, and table at the time of the operation
- `changes` — field-level diff with explicit `old`/`new` for every operation:
  - **INSERT**: `old` is always `null`
  - **UPDATE**: both `old` and `new` reflect the changed values
  - **REMOVE**: empty by default; with `full_snapshot_on_remove`, every audited field with its `old` value and a `null` `new` (a generated identifier, reset by Doctrine on deletion, is left out: the `source` block holds it), and every owning-side to-one association with the summary of its target as `old`
- `snapshot` — only on entries written by [`audit:snapshot`](#auditsnapshot): an `insert` entry with
  `"snapshot": true` records the state of an entity that existed before auditing started, not its creation
  (`Entry::isSnapshot()` reads it)
- **ASSOCIATE / DISSOCIATE** — use a different structure (no `changes` key):
  ```json
  {
      "source":       { "id": "1", "class": "App\\Entity\\Post", "label": "Post #1", "table": "posts", "field": "tags" },
      "target":       { "id": "5", "class": "App\\Entity\\Tag",  "label": "php",     "table": "tag",   "field": "posts" },
      "is_owning_side": true,
      "join_table":   "post__tag"
  }
  ```

#### Legacy Diffs Format (schema version 1)

Entries written by earlier versions of the provider carry `schema_version = 1`. The `Entry` model reads them transparently — see [Entry Reference](../../querying/entry.md).

#### Writing audit rows yourself

The provider writes audit rows on flush only. An application that writes rows itself (for example to import the
history kept by another tool) must follow the format above, or the `Reader` and the viewer misread the rows without
any error:

| Column | What to write |
|---|---|
| `schema_version` | `2`, always written explicitly: do not rely on the column default, which can still be `1` on a table left half-migrated or completed by hand; a row read as `1` has its diffs read as the legacy format |
| `type` | `insert`, `update`, `remove`, `associate` or `dissociate` |
| `object_id`, `discriminator` | the identifier of the entity as a string; its class in `discriminator` for an entity of an inheritance hierarchy, `NULL` otherwise |
| `transaction_id` | a ULID (26 characters, e.g. `(string) new Ulid()` with `symfony/uid`), the same for every row written by one flush (one transaction), across tables: the viewer and `Query::transactions()` group the entries by it |
| `diffs` | the envelope `{"source": {…}, "changes": {"field": {"old": …, "new": …}}}`, or the association structure; `source` holds `id`, `class`, `label` and `table`; plus `deep_diffs` (the fields whose change is a JSON deep diff) when relevant, without which the deep diffs are inferred from their shape |
| `blame_id`, `blame` | `NULL` and `NULL` when nobody is known; otherwise `blame` holds the four keys `username`, `user_fqdn`, `user_firewall` and `ip`, each set to `null` when unknown, plus `impersonator` and `via` when relevant |
| `extra_data` | a JSON object, or `NULL` |
| `created_at` | the date of the change, `Y-m-d H:i:s`, in the timezone of the configuration (`timezone`, UTC by default) |

- `diffs`, `blame` and `extra_data` are `JSONB` on PostgreSQL: cast the values (`::jsonb`) in a hand-written
  `INSERT`.
- Rows written by hand go around the `LifecycleEvent` listeners of the application (extra data, rewriting of the
  diffs): apply their effect yourself.
- Rows of entities that declare an [`#[AuditRoot]`](../../querying/history.md) are not indexed in `audit_root`: run
  [`audit:roots:rebuild`](#auditrootsrebuild) after the import, or they are missing from the histories.

### 🛠️ Using SchemaManager

#### Creating the Schema Manager

```php
<?php

use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Schema\SchemaManager;

$schemaManager = new SchemaManager($provider);
```

#### Updating the Schema (Manual)

Creates audit tables for entities that don't have one yet, and adds missing columns to existing ones:

```php
// Create / update all audit tables
$schemaManager->updateAuditSchema();
```

> [!NOTE]
> `updateAuditSchema()` is safe to run repeatedly. It checks for existing tables and columns before making changes.

#### Console Commands

Six console commands are available.

##### `audit:schema:update`

Creates new audit tables and updates existing ones to match the current schema.

```bash
# Preview the SQL that would be executed
php bin/console audit:schema:update --dump-sql

# Execute the changes
php bin/console audit:schema:update --force

# Both: show SQL and execute
php bin/console audit:schema:update --dump-sql --force
```

##### `audit:schema:migrate`

Migrates existing audit tables from schema version 1 to schema version 2.

```bash
# Preview the SQL that would be executed (dry-run)
php bin/console audit:schema:migrate --dump-sql --convert-all

# Execute the migration and convert the existing rows (recommended)
php bin/console audit:schema:migrate --force --convert-all

# Convert a sample only, to estimate the duration (keeps the legacy columns, resumable)
php bin/console audit:schema:migrate --force --convert-all --limit=10000
```

> [!CAUTION]
> The migration drops the legacy columns and cannot be undone: back up the audit tables first. `transaction_hash` is
> only dropped once converted (`--convert-transaction-hash` or `--convert-all`), or with `--drop-transaction-hash`,
> which drops it without converting it: legacy rows then lose their transaction grouping. Follow the
> [upgrade guide](../../upgrade/v2.md#-upgrade-steps) for the complete procedure.

> [!NOTE]
> Use `audit:schema:migrate` when upgrading an existing installation. New installations created
> with `audit:schema:update` already use schema version 2.

> [!NOTE]
> `--convert-diffs` rewrites existing diffs rows in PHP (batches of 500). This can take a while
> on large tables. Without this flag, legacy rows remain readable via `Entry::getDiffs()` since
> the `Entry` model handles both schema versions transparently.

##### `audit:clean`

Removes audit entries older than a specified retention period (`P12M` by default).

```bash
# Keep last 6 months (dry run)
php bin/console audit:clean P6M --dry-run

# Execute, skip confirmation (for cron jobs)
php bin/console audit:clean P12M --no-confirm

# Delete before a specific date
php bin/console audit:clean --date=2024-01-01 --no-confirm

# Exclude specific entities
php bin/console audit:clean -x App\\Entity\\User

# Include only specific entities
php bin/console audit:clean -i App\\Entity\\Log
```

Entities with a retention policy (`#[Auditable(maxAge: …, maxEntries: …)]`, or the `max_age` / `max_entries` entity
options) apply it: `maxAge` replaces the global cutoff, and `maxEntries` also deletes everything but the N most recent
entries. See [Retention Policy](attributes.md#retention-policy).

##### `audit:export`

Exports audit entries as NDJSON (default, recommended for large exports), JSON or CSV, streamed to the standard
output or to a file.

```bash
# Every auditable entity, NDJSON on stdout
php bin/console audit:export

# One entity, as CSV, for a period
php bin/console audit:export App\\Entity\\Post --format=csv --from=2026-01-01 --to=2026-03-31 --output=posts.csv

# One object, or one user, without the user and IP fields
php bin/console audit:export App\\Entity\\Post --id=42 --anonymize
php bin/console audit:export --blame-id=7
```

Each line or row is an `Entry::toArray()`: the same columns for legacy and schema v2 entries.

##### `audit:roots:rebuild`

Indexes the existing audit entries under their audit roots (`#[AuditRoot]`, `roots` entity option), in the
`audit_root` table: after declaring a new root, or after migrating audit tables to schema v2.

```bash
php bin/console audit:roots:rebuild
php bin/console audit:roots:rebuild --entity='App\Entity\Comment' --dry-run
```

| Option      | Description                                                    |
|-------------|----------------------------------------------------------------|
| `--entity`  | Entities whose entries are indexed (repeatable), all by default |
| `--dry-run` | Count the missing index rows, write nothing                    |

Only missing rows are written and no row is deleted, so the command can be run again and rows written by hand are
kept. See
[Histories](../../querying/history.md#rebuilding-the-index).

##### `audit:snapshot`

Records the current state of existing entities, so that their history does not start at their first change
when auditing is enabled on a database that already holds data. Each entity gets one `insert` entry flagged
with `"snapshot": true`, holding the current value of every audited field (`old: null`).

```bash
# Snapshot some entities
php bin/console audit:snapshot 'App\Entity\Post' 'App\Entity\Author'

# Snapshot every audited entity, 1,000 rows per database transaction
php bin/console audit:snapshot --all --batch-size=1000

# Count what would be written
php bin/console audit:snapshot --all --dry-run
```

| Option         | Short | Description                                                                  |
|----------------|-------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `--all`        | `-a`  | Snapshot every audited entity (instead of the entities given as arguments)   |
| `--batch-size` | `-b`  | Entities read and written per database transaction (default `500`)           |
| `--force`      | `-f`  | Also snapshot entities that already have an audit history                    |
| `--dry-run`    |       | Count the entities to snapshot, write nothing                                |

- **Idempotent**: an entity that already has at least one audit entry is skipped, so the command can be
  run again (e.g. after an interruption). `--force` snapshots it anyway: a manual snapshot of its current state.
- **Batches**: entities are read in identifier order (keyset pagination), each batch is written in its own
  database transaction and its entries share one `transaction_id`. The entity manager is cleared between batches.
- **Content**: the same fields as an insert: ignored columns and generated identifiers are left out,
  owning-side to-one associations are summarized, JSON fields are deep diffs. To-many associations are not
  snapshotted.
- **Context**: `created_at` is the date of the snapshot, the blame is the console user (`blame_id` is `null`
  without a user provider). Doctrine filters that are enabled apply: rows they hide (e.g. soft-deleted) are
  not snapshotted.
- **Inheritance**: an entity whose parent class is also selected is read through its parent; each row is
  written to the audit table of its own class.

The same logic is available in PHP through `DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Auditing\Snapshot\Snapshotter`:

```php
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Auditing\Snapshot\Snapshotter;

$result = new Snapshotter($provider)->snapshot(Post::class, batchSize: 500);
$result->read;        // entities read
$result->snapshotted; // entries written
$result->skipped();   // entities that already had an audit history
```

> [!NOTE]
> These commands use Symfony's Lock component to prevent concurrent execution.

##### Registering Commands (Standalone)

When not using auditor-bundle, register the commands manually:

```php
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Command\CleanAuditLogsCommand;
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Command\ExportAuditLogsCommand;
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Command\MigrateSchemaCommand;
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Command\RebuildRootsCommand;
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Command\SnapshotCommand;
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Command\UpdateSchemaCommand;
use Symfony\Component\Console\Application;

$application = new Application();

foreach ([
    new UpdateSchemaCommand(),
    new MigrateSchemaCommand(),
    new CleanAuditLogsCommand(),
    new SnapshotCommand(),
    new ExportAuditLogsCommand(),
    new RebuildRootsCommand(),
] as $command) {
    $application->addCommand($command->setAuditor($auditor));
}

$application->run();
```

#### Programmatic Schema Update

```php
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Schema\SchemaManager;

$schemaManager = new SchemaManager($provider);

// Get SQL without executing
$sqls = $schemaManager->getUpdateAuditSchemaSql();

// Execute all pending changes
$schemaManager->updateAuditSchema();

// Execute with a progress callback
$schemaManager->updateAuditSchema(null, function (array $progress) {
    echo sprintf('Progress: %d / %d', $progress['current'], $progress['total']);
});
```

### 📛 Table Naming

#### Default Naming

By default, audit tables are named: `{entity_table}_audit`

| Entity Table | Audit Table       |
|--------------|-------------------|
| `users`      | `users_audit`     |
| `posts`      | `posts_audit`     |
| `blog_posts` | `blog_posts_audit`|

#### Custom Prefix/Suffix

```php
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Configuration;

// Prefix only: audit_posts
$config = new Configuration([
    'table_prefix' => 'audit_',
    'table_suffix' => '',
]);

// Suffix only: posts_history
$config = new Configuration([
    'table_prefix' => '',
    'table_suffix' => '_history',
]);

// Both: audit_posts_log
$config = new Configuration([
    'table_prefix' => 'audit_',
    'table_suffix' => '_log',
]);
```

### 🔄 Schema Changes

#### Adding a New Audited Entity

When you add `#[Auditable]` to a new entity and add it to the configuration:

1. Call `$schemaManager->updateAuditSchema()` to create the new audit table.

#### Removing an Audited Entity

> [!NOTE]
> When you remove an entity from the auditing configuration, the audit table is **not** automatically deleted. Historical data is preserved. Drop the table manually if you no longer need it.

#### Modifying Entity Fields

> [!TIP]
> Adding or removing fields from an entity requires **no schema changes** to the audit table. Diffs are stored as JSON, so new fields appear in future audits automatically and removed fields simply won't appear in new entries.

### 🗄️ Database-Specific Notes

#### MySQL / MariaDB

- Native `JSON` column type is used for `diffs`, `extra_data`, and `blame`
- InnoDB engine is recommended for transactional integrity
- InnoDB does not compress anything by default. On **MariaDB**, enable the [`compression`](configuration.md#-compression)
  option to store `diffs` and `extra_data` as compressed columns (`JSON COMPRESSED`).
- **MySQL** has no column compression, so the `compression` option has no effect there. If disk space matters more
  than speed, InnoDB page compression can be enabled manually on audit tables (requires `innodb_file_per_table` and a
  file system supporting hole punching, e.g. ext4 or XFS):

  ```sql
  ALTER TABLE posts_audit COMPRESSION='zlib';
  OPTIMIZE TABLE posts_audit; -- compresses existing rows
  ```

  Doctrine does not manage table compression options: this is neither reported nor reverted by schema commands.

#### PostgreSQL

- Native `JSONB` column type is used for `diffs`, `extra_data` and `blame`
- Large `JSONB` values are compressed automatically (TOAST): the `compression` option is not needed and has no effect
- Audit tables created with `JSON` columns by previous versions are converted to `JSONB` by `audit:schema:update` (or by your next migration if you manage audit tables with Doctrine Migrations)
- Indexed columns use PostgreSQL-compatible index names

#### SQLite

> [!NOTE]
> SQLite is recommended for development and testing only. It supports JSON operations natively from version 3.38+.

### ⚡ Performance Considerations

1. **Few indexes** — `(object_id, type)` and `(blame_id, created_at)` cover the most frequent Reader query patterns, and every
   other secondary index slows each audit `INSERT` down: there is none on `object_id`, `blame_id` or `discriminator`
   alone (5 secondary indexes instead of 8 before 2.0: audit `INSERT`s about 18 % faster on MySQL, indexes 30 % smaller)
2. **JSON storage** — Native JSON types (MySQL, PostgreSQL) provide best query performance on `diffs` and `blame`
3. **Archiving** — Implement a periodic cleanup strategy for high-volume applications using `audit:clean`
4. **Separate database** — Consider storing audits in a dedicated database to avoid impacting application performance

---

- 🔍 [Querying Audits](../../querying/index.md)
- 🗄️ [Multi-Database Setup](multi-database.md)
- 💡 [Extra Data](../../extra-data.md)

## Services

> **AuditingService and StorageService — the building blocks of the DoctrineProvider**

The DoctrineProvider relies on two types of services: **AuditingService** (source of changes) and **StorageService** (destination of audit entries).

### 🔍 Overview

| Service           | Interface                  | Responsibility                                              |
|-------------------|----------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|
| `AuditingService` | `AuditingServiceInterface` | Wraps an EntityManager and captures entity changes          |
| `StorageService`  | `StorageServiceInterface`  | Wraps an EntityManager used to persist audit entries        |

Both services extend `DoctrineService` and wrap a Doctrine `EntityManagerInterface`.

### 🔌 AuditingService

The `AuditingService` wraps the EntityManager whose entities should be audited.

When `DoctrineProvider::registerAuditingService()` is called, it registers the `DoctrineSubscriber` on the event manager of the entity manager. The `AuditorMiddleware` is **not** added for you: it must be in the middlewares of the DBAL connection (see below).

#### Namespace

```php
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Service\AuditingService;
```

#### Constructor

```php
$auditingService = new AuditingService(
    'default',       // Service name
    $entityManager   // Doctrine\ORM\EntityManagerInterface
);
```

#### Registration

```php
$provider->registerAuditingService($auditingService);
// ↑ This attaches DoctrineSubscriber to the event manager of the entity manager (onFlush, postFlush).
//   The connection must have been created with the AuditorMiddleware.
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The EntityManager must be configured **before** the provider is registered with the auditor. The `AuditorMiddleware` must be present in the DBAL middleware stack for the transactional flush callback to work: without it, nothing is audited.
>
> ```php
> $dbalConfiguration = new \Doctrine\DBAL\Configuration();
> $dbalConfiguration->setMiddlewares([new \DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Auditing\DBAL\Middleware\AuditorMiddleware()]);
> $connection = \Doctrine\DBAL\DriverManager::getConnection($connectionParams, $dbalConfiguration);
> ```
>
> auditor-bundle adds it to the connections of the auditing entity managers.

#### Attaching the listeners yourself

`registerAuditingService()` attaches the listeners when it runs, that is when the provider is built: a flush run before
that is not audited. A dependency injection container can declare them instead, as lazy listeners of the event
managers: they are registered with the event manager when it is created, and the provider is built on the first flush
(auditor-bundle does it):

```php
$provider->disableListenerAttachment();   // before registerAuditingService()
$provider->registerAuditingService(new AuditingService('default', $entityManager));

// then, on the event manager of each auditing entity manager:
// - $provider->getDoctrineSubscriber() on onFlush, postFlush (and Gedmo's postSoftDelete)
// - new CreateSchemaListener($provider) on postGenerateSchemaTable
// (TableSchemaListener does nothing any more: it is not needed)
```

The subscriber is shared by all the auditing entity managers, whose state it keeps apart: entity managers sharing an
event manager (as on one DoctrineBundle connection) get it once.

> [!WARNING]
> Before 6.4.44, 7.4.17 and 8.1.5, the `ContainerAwareEventManager` of Symfony's doctrine-bridge drops a listener
> attached while it initializes its lazy listeners of the same event: a lazy `onFlush` listener that only builds the
> provider would lose the subscriber. Declare the subscriber itself as the listener.

### 💾 StorageService

The `StorageService` wraps the EntityManager used to write audit rows. This can be the same EntityManager as the auditing service (single database) or a different one (multi-database).

#### Namespace

```php
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Service\StorageService;
```

#### Constructor

```php
$storageService = new StorageService(
    'default',       // Service name
    $entityManager   // Doctrine\ORM\EntityManagerInterface
);
```

#### Registration

```php
$provider->registerStorageService($storageService);
```

### 🔗 Single Database Setup

The most common setup uses the same EntityManager for both services:

```php
<?php

use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Service\AuditingService;
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Service\StorageService;

$provider->registerAuditingService(new AuditingService('default', $entityManager));
$provider->registerStorageService(new StorageService('default', $entityManager));
```

### 🗄️ Multi-Database Setup

For multi-database setups, register multiple services with distinct names and configure a storage mapper:

```php
<?php

use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Service\AuditingService;
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Service\StorageService;

// $appEntityManager reads/writes your application data
// $auditEntityManager writes audit rows to a separate database

$provider->registerAuditingService(
    new AuditingService('app', $appEntityManager)
);

$provider->registerStorageService(
    new StorageService('audit', $auditEntityManager)
);
```

> [!NOTE]
> See [Multi-Database](multi-database.md) for a complete guide including the `storage_mapper` callback.

### 🔎 Retrieving Services

```php
// Get all registered auditing services
$auditingServices = $provider->getAuditingServices();

// Get all registered storage services
$storageServices = $provider->getStorageServices();

// Get the underlying EntityManager from a service
$em = $storageService->getEntityManager();
```

---

### ♻️ Long-Running Processes (Symfony Messenger Workers)

When running auditor inside **Symfony Messenger workers**, the EntityManager is reset between messages by Symfony's `services_resetter`. Without proper handling, only the first message is audited correctly — subsequent messages silently fail because:

- The `DoctrineSubscriber` would hold a stale EntityManager reference.
- The `DoctrineProvider` would reuse cached `PreparedStatement` objects bound to a closed connection.

`DoctrineProvider` implements `Symfony\Contracts\Service\ResetInterface`. Its `reset()` method clears the prepared statement cache and resets all subscriber transaction caches, ensuring clean state between messages.

#### Wiring `kernel.reset` in Symfony

For Symfony to call `reset()` automatically between messages, tag `DoctrineProvider` with `kernel.reset`:

**With `autoconfigure: true` (recommended)**

If your service definition uses `autoconfigure: true`, Symfony detects `ResetInterface` and registers the tag automatically — no additional config needed.

**Manual tag**

```yaml
# config/services.yaml
services:
    DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\DoctrineProvider:
        tags:
            - { name: kernel.reset, method: reset }
```

> [!NOTE]
> If you use `damienharper/auditor-bundle`, check the bundle's documentation for its service configuration — the tag may already be applied.

---

- 🗄️ [Multi-Database Setup](multi-database.md)
- 🛠️ [Schema Management](schema.md)
- ⚙️ [Configuration Reference](configuration.md)

## Entry Reference

> **The audit log entry model**

An `Entry` object represents a single audit log record. It is returned by `Query::execute()` and is part of the `damienharper/auditor` core library.

### 📦 The Entry Class

```php
use DH\Auditor\Model\Entry;
```

`Entry` is a read-only value object hydrated from a database row.

### 📋 Virtual Properties

`Entry` exposes its data through **virtual properties** (not getter methods). Access them directly:

| Property         | Type                   | Description                                                          |
|------------------|------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `$id`            | `int`                  | Auto-increment primary key of the audit entry                        |
| `$schemaVersion` | `int`                  | Diffs format version: `1` (legacy) or `2` (current). Defaults to `1`.|
| `$type`          | `string`               | Action type: `insert`, `update`, `remove`, `associate`, `dissociate` |
| `$objectId`      | `string`               | Primary key of the audited entity                                    |
| `$discriminator` | `string\|null`         | Entity class (used in inheritance hierarchies)                       |
| `$transactionId` | `string\|null`         | ULID grouping changes from the same flush batch                      |
| `$extraData`     | `array\|null`          | Already-decoded extra data (do **not** call `json_decode()`)         |
| `$userId`        | `int\|string\|null`    | Identifier of the user who made the change (`blame_id`)              |
| `$blame`         | `array\|null`          | Decoded blame context: `username`, `user_fqdn`, `user_firewall`, `ip`, plus `impersonator` and `via` when set |
| `$username`      | `string\|null`         | Convenience shortcut for `$blame['username']`                        |
| `$userFqdn`      | `string\|null`         | Convenience shortcut for `$blame['user_fqdn']`                       |
| `$userFirewall`  | `string\|null`         | Convenience shortcut for `$blame['user_firewall']`                   |
| `$ip`            | `string\|null`         | Convenience shortcut for `$blame['ip']`                              |
| `$impersonator`  | `array\|null`          | User who impersonated the blamed one (`id`, `username`, `fqdn`), from `$blame['impersonator']` |
| `$via`           | `array\|null`          | Blame context (`type`, `label`, `data`) the change was made in, from `$blame['via']` |
| `$createdAt`     | `\DateTimeImmutable`   | Timestamp of when the audit entry was created                        |
| `$entity`        | `string\|null`         | FQCN of the audited entity, set by readers that merge several audit tables (history of a root) |
| `$rootPath`      | `string\|null`         | Path that led to the root in the history of a root (`null` for the root itself) |

`isDeepDiff($field)` tells whether a field's changeset is a JSON deep diff, and `getSortKey()` gives a total order
of entries across tables (see [Histories](history.md)).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> - `$entry->type` is a plain `string` (e.g. `'insert'`, `'update'`), not an enum.
> - `$entry->extraData` is **already decoded** — it returns `?array`. Never call `json_decode()` on it.

### 🔍 Reading Diffs

Use `getDiffs()` to access the field-level change data:

```php
$audits = $reader->createQuery(Post::class, ['object_id' => 42])->execute();

foreach ($audits as $entry) {
    // getDiffs() returns the 'changes' sub-array for schema v2 entries
    // and the raw diff array for legacy schema v1 entries
    foreach ($entry->getDiffs() as $field => $change) {
        $old = $change['old'] ?? '(null)';
        $new = $change['new'] ?? '(null)';
        echo "  $field: $old → $new\n";
    }
}
```

#### Diff Structure (schema version 2)

All entry types use the same unified envelope. `getDiffs()` returns the `changes` sub-array directly.

**`insert`** — `old` is always `null`:
```json
{
    "title":   { "old": null, "new": "Hello World" },
    "content": { "old": null, "new": "My first post." }
}
```

**`update`**:
```json
{
    "title": { "old": "Hello World", "new": "Hello auditor!" }
}
```

**`remove`** — empty by default (the `source` block identifies the deleted entity); with the `full_snapshot_on_remove` option, every audited field and owning-side to-one association, `new` always `null` (except a generated identifier, which only the `source` block holds):
```json
{
    "title":   { "old": "Hello auditor!", "new": null },
    "content": { "old": "My first post.", "new": null },
    "author":  { "old": { "id": 1, "class": "App\\Entity\\Author", "label": "John", "table": "author" }, "new": null }
}
```

**`associate` / `dissociate`** — no `changes` key; `getDiffs()` returns the full envelope:
```json
{
    "source":         { "id": "1", "class": "App\\Entity\\Post", "label": "Post #1", "table": "posts", "field": "tags" },
    "target":         { "id": "5", "class": "App\\Entity\\Tag",  "label": "php",     "table": "tag",   "field": "posts" },
    "is_owning_side": true,
    "join_table":     "post__tag"
}
```

#### Source and Target Metadata

For schema v2 entries, use `getDiffSource()` and `getDiffTarget()`:

```php
// getDiffSource(): entity metadata at the time of the operation (all types)
$source = $entry->getDiffSource();
// ['class' => 'App\Entity\Post', 'id' => '42', 'label' => 'Hello World', 'table' => 'posts']

// getDiffTarget(): second entity in associate/dissociate entries
$target = $entry->getDiffTarget();
// ['class' => 'App\Entity\Tag', 'field' => 'posts', 'id' => '5', 'label' => 'php', 'table' => 'tag']
```

Both return `null` for legacy schema v1 entries.

#### Snapshots

`audit:snapshot` records the state of entities that existed before auditing started as `insert` entries
flagged with `"snapshot": true`. `isSnapshot()` tells them from real insertions (always `false` on schema v1):

```php
if ('insert' === $entry->type && $entry->isSnapshot()) {
    // state of the entity at $entry->createdAt, when it was snapshotted: not its creation
}
```

#### Legacy Diff Structure (schema version 1)

`getDiffs()` returns the raw decoded array as-is, minus the internal `@source` key that legacy inserts carry
(`getDiffSource()` returns `null` for legacy entries):

**`insert`** (as returned by `getDiffs()`):
```json
{
    "title":   { "new": "Hello World" },
    "content": { "new": "My first post." }
}
```

**`update`**:
```json
{
    "title": { "old": "Hello World", "new": "Hello auditor!" }
}
```

**`remove`**:
```json
{
    "id":    42,
    "class": "App\\Entity\\Post",
    "label": "Hello auditor!",
    "table": "posts"
}
```

### 💡 Reading Extra Data

```php
// $entry->extraData is already decoded — no json_decode() needed
if (null !== $entry->extraData) {
    echo 'Reason: ' . ($entry->extraData['reason'] ?? 'unknown') . "\n";
}
```

### 📅 Timezone Handling

The `$createdAt` property is a `\DateTimeImmutable` object. Its timezone is set to the timezone configured in the auditor `Configuration`:

```php
$configuration = new Configuration(['timezone' => 'Europe/Paris']);

// ...

foreach ($entries as $entry) {
    $dt = $entry->createdAt;
    echo $dt->format('Y-m-d H:i:s T'); // e.g., 2024-06-15 14:30:00 CEST
}
```

### 📝 Full Example

```php
<?php

use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Reader;

$reader = new Reader($provider);
$entries = $reader->createQuery(App\Entity\Post::class, [
    'object_id' => 42,
    'page'      => 1,
    'page_size' => 10,
])->execute();

foreach ($entries as $entry) {
    $source = $entry->getDiffSource();

    printf(
        "[%s] %s #%s — by %s (%s) from %s at %s\n",
        $entry->type,
        $source['class'] ?? App\Entity\Post::class,
        $entry->objectId,
        $entry->username ?? 'anonymous',
        $entry->userId ?? '-',
        $entry->ip ?? '-',
        $entry->createdAt->format('Y-m-d H:i:s')
    );

    foreach ($entry->getDiffs() as $field => $change) {
        if (!\is_array($change) || $entry->isDeepDiff($field)) {
            continue;   // association entries and JSON deep diffs have another shape
        }
        printf("  %s: %s → %s\n", $field, json_encode($change['old'] ?? null), json_encode($change['new'] ?? null));
    }
}
```

- 🔍 [Querying Audits](index.md)
- 🔧 [Filters Reference](filters.md)
- 💡 [Extra Data](../extra-data.md)

## Filters Reference

> **Fine-grained control over audit queries**

Filters allow you to restrict the results returned by a `Query`. They can be added via `createQuery()` options or directly on the `Query` object.

### 📋 Available Filters

| Filter             | Class             | Description                                    |
|--------------------|-------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| `SimpleFilter`     | `SimpleFilter`    | Equality or `IN` match on a column             |
| `DateRangeFilter`  | `DateRangeFilter` | Filter by a date range on a datetime column    |
| `RangeFilter`      | `RangeFilter`     | Filter by a numeric range                      |
| `NullFilter`       | `NullFilter`      | Filter for NULL / NOT NULL values              |
| `JsonFilter`       | `JsonFilter`      | Filter by a value inside a JSON column, typically `extra_data` |
| `ChangedFieldFilter` | `ChangedFieldFilter` | Entries whose diff touches a given field (or one of several) |
| `BlameOriginFilter` | `BlameOriginFilter` | Entries made from some origins: web request, console, worker, system |
| `ImpersonatorFilter` | `ImpersonatorFilter` | Entries made while a user impersonated another one, optionally by a given impersonator |
| `RootFilter`       | `RootFilter`      | Entries indexed under an audit root (see [Histories](history.md)) |

All filter classes live under:

```php
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Filter\{FilterClass};
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Query;
```

### 🔵 SimpleFilter

Matches a single value or a list of values (generates `= ?` or `IN (?,?)` SQL).

#### Usage

```php
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Filter\SimpleFilter;
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Query;

// Match a single value
$query->addFilter(new SimpleFilter(Query::TYPE, 'update'));

// Match multiple values (IN clause)
$query->addFilter(new SimpleFilter(Query::TYPE, ['insert', 'update']));

// Filter by user ID
$query->addFilter(new SimpleFilter(Query::USER_ID, 'user-42'));

// Filter by entity ID
$query->addFilter(new SimpleFilter(Query::OBJECT_ID, '100'));
```

#### Supported Columns

| Constant                    | Column           |
|-----------------------------|------------------|
| `Query::ID`                 | `id`             |
| `Query::TYPE`               | `type`           |
| `Query::OBJECT_ID`          | `object_id`      |
| `Query::DISCRIMINATOR`      | `discriminator`  |
| `Query::TRANSACTION_ID`     | `transaction_id` |
| `Query::USER_ID`            | `blame_id`       |

> [!NOTE]
> `Query::TRANSACTION_HASH` is kept for backward compatibility and maps to `transaction_id`
> (same as `Query::TRANSACTION_ID`). Use `Query::TRANSACTION_ID` in new code.

### 📅 DateRangeFilter

Filters entries by a date range on `created_at`.

#### Usage

```php
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Filter\DateRangeFilter;
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Query;

// Entries created in January 2024
$query->addFilter(new DateRangeFilter(
    Query::CREATED_AT,
    new \DateTimeImmutable('2024-01-01'),
    new \DateTimeImmutable('2024-01-31')
));

// Entries created after a given date (open end)
$query->addFilter(new DateRangeFilter(
    Query::CREATED_AT,
    new \DateTimeImmutable('2024-06-01'),
    null
));

// Entries created before a given date (open start)
$query->addFilter(new DateRangeFilter(
    Query::CREATED_AT,
    null,
    new \DateTimeImmutable('2024-06-01')
));
```

### 🔢 RangeFilter

Filters entries by a numeric range (e.g., `id` between two values).

#### Usage

```php
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Filter\RangeFilter;
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Query;

// Entries with ID between 100 and 200
$query->addFilter(new RangeFilter(Query::ID, 100, 200));

// IDs greater than 500 (open end)
$query->addFilter(new RangeFilter(Query::ID, 500, null));
```

### ❌ NullFilter

Filters entries where a column is `NULL` or `NOT NULL`.

#### Usage

```php
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Filter\NullFilter;
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Query;

// Entries where blame_id IS NULL (anonymous changes)
$query->addFilter(new NullFilter(Query::USER_ID));
```

`NullFilter` only tests `IS NULL`. To keep the entries whose column is not null, use a `RangeFilter` or a
`SimpleFilter` with the values you expect, or a `JsonFilter` with `IS NOT NULL` on a JSON column.

> [!WARNING]
> `NullFilter` works on indexed columns such as `blame_id`, `object_id`, `type`, etc. Do not use `Query::JSON` with `NullFilter` — there is no `json` column in the audit table. To find entries where `extra_data IS NULL`, query without a filter and check `$entry->extraData === null`.

### 🔍 JsonFilter

Filters entries on a value inside a JSON column, typically `extra_data`:
`new JsonFilter($column, $path, $value = null, $operator = '=', $strict = false)`.

#### Usage

```php
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Filter\JsonFilter;

// Entries whose extra_data.department is 'IT'
$query->addFilter(new JsonFilter('extra_data', 'department', 'IT'));

// Entries whose extra_data has a non-null 'route'
$query->addFilter(new JsonFilter('extra_data', 'route', null, 'IS NOT NULL'));
```

Operators: `=`, `!=`, `<>`, `LIKE`, `NOT LIKE`, `IN`, `NOT IN`, `IS NULL`, `IS NOT NULL`. On a platform without JSON
support, the filter falls back to `LIKE` unless `$strict` is `true` (it then throws). See
[Extra Data](../extra-data.md#filtering-by-extra-data) for the platforms and indexing.

> [!TIP]
> To find the entries that changed a field, use [`ChangedFieldFilter`](#-changedfieldfilter) rather than a
> `JsonFilter` on `diffs`.

### ✏️ ChangedFieldFilter

Restricts the results to the entries whose diff touches a given field, whatever the operation:

- inserts and updates that changed the field;
- removes recorded with `full_snapshot_on_remove` enabled (removes without a snapshot carry no field);
- associations and dissociations recorded on the field, so that filtering on a collection returns the items added to or removed from it.

Both diff formats are read: the schema v2 envelope (including the rows converted by `audit:schema:migrate --convert-diffs`) and the legacy rows (`schema_version = 1`) that were not converted yet.

#### Usage

```php
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Filter\ChangedFieldFilter;

// Through the createQuery() option
$query = $reader->createQuery(Post::class, ['changed_field' => 'title']);

// Or directly on the query
$query->addFilter(new ChangedFieldFilter('tags'));

// Fields of embeddables use their dotted name
$query->addFilter(new ChangedFieldFilter('address.street'));

// Entries that changed any of several fields
$query = $reader->createQuery(Post::class, ['changed_field' => ['title', 'body']]);
```

The field name must be a Doctrine field name (letters, digits and underscores, dotted for embeddables), otherwise an `InvalidArgumentException` is thrown. It is always passed to the database as a bound parameter.

> [!NOTE]
> `ChangedFieldFilter` requires native JSON support (MySQL 5.7+, MariaDB 10.2.3+, PostgreSQL 9.4+, SQLite 3.38+) and an audit table with the schema v2 structure: run `audit:schema:migrate` on legacy tables first. It throws an `InvalidArgumentException` otherwise; check `JsonPlatformHelper::isJsonSearchSupported()` beforehand to offer the filter only where it works.

> [!TIP]
> The predicate cannot use an index: the database reads the `diffs` of every row left by the other filters. Combine it with `object_id` or a date range on large audit tables.

### 🧭 BlameOriginFilter

Keeps the entries made from some origins (`DH\Auditor\History\BlameOrigin`): `http` (a web request with a
firewall), `console`, `messenger` (blame context types) or `system` (anything else). Several origins are combined
with `OR`. It reads the `blame` JSON column, so it needs native JSON support and a schema v2 table.

```php
use DH\Auditor\History\BlameOrigin;
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Filter\BlameOriginFilter;

$query->addFilter(new BlameOriginFilter([BlameOrigin::Console, BlameOrigin::Messenger]));

// Or through the createQuery() option
$query = $reader->createQuery(Post::class, ['blame_origin' => 'http']);
```

### 🎭 ImpersonatorFilter

Keeps the entries made while a user impersonated another one (switch user): those whose `blame` JSON has an
`impersonator` key, written when the user provider returns a user with an impersonator. Given an identifier, it
keeps those of that impersonator only. It reads the `blame` JSON column, so it needs native JSON support and a
schema v2 table.

```php
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Filter\ImpersonatorFilter;

$query->addFilter(new ImpersonatorFilter());     // made by impersonating someone
$query->addFilter(new ImpersonatorFilter('1'));  // made by impersonator #1
```

Entries written before the `impersonator` key existed are not found: auditor-bundle before 8.0 appended the
impersonator to the username instead (`alice[impersonator admin]`).

### 🌳 RootFilter

Keeps the entries indexed under an audit root, optionally through some paths only. It reads the `audit_root` index
table: use it through `Reader::createRootQuery()`, which sets the index table and merges the tables of every entity
(see [Histories](history.md)).

### 🔗 Combining Filters

Multiple filters are combined with `AND`:

```php
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Filter\{DateRangeFilter, SimpleFilter};
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Query;

$query = $reader->createQuery(Post::class);

// All updates by user '42' in the last 30 days
$query->addFilter(new SimpleFilter(Query::TYPE, 'update'));
$query->addFilter(new SimpleFilter(Query::USER_ID, '42'));
$query->addFilter(new DateRangeFilter(
    Query::CREATED_AT,
    new \DateTimeImmutable('-30 days'),
    null
));

$entries = $query->execute();
```

### 📐 Ordering Results

```php
// Default order: created_at DESC, id DESC
// Override:
$query->addOrderBy(Query::CREATED_AT, 'ASC');
$query->addOrderBy(Query::ID, 'ASC');
```

### 📄 Manual Pagination

```php
// 20 results starting at offset 40 (page 3 of 20 per page)
$query->limit(20, 40);
$entries = $query->execute();
```

- 🔍 [Querying Audits](index.md)
- 📦 [Entry Reference](entry.md)

## Histories (Querying)

> **Read the history of a business object across several audit tables, and the last change of each field**

The building blocks (`#[AuditRoot]`, `HistoryGrouper`, `ChangeExtractor`, `BlameOrigin`) are described in the
[auditor documentation](https://damienharper.github.io/auditor-docs/auditor/history). This page covers what the
Doctrine provider adds: the audit root index, the history of a root, and field-level queries.

### 🌳 Declaring roots

With the `#[AuditRoot]` attribute, or the `roots` entity option (both are merged):

```php
use DH\Auditor\Attribute\Auditable;
use DH\Auditor\Attribute\AuditRoot;

#[ORM\Entity]
#[Auditable]
#[AuditRoot('property')]
#[AuditRoot('visit.property')]
class VisitReport { /* … */ }
```

```php
$configuration = new Configuration([
    'entities' => [
        App\Entity\VisitReport::class => ['roots' => ['property', 'visit.property']],
    ],
]);
```

A path is a list of **single-valued** association properties (`ManyToOne`, `OneToOne`, owning or inverse side)
separated by dots. A collection in a path is an error, raised at the first flush of the entity. Roots declared on a
parent class are inherited.

For roots that a path cannot express (a polymorphic owner stored as a class and an id, a root picked by business
rules), give the provider a `root_resolver`: a callable that receives an audited entity and returns its extra roots,
keyed by a name of your choice, written as the root path of the index rows (null roots are skipped):

```php
$configuration->setRootResolver(static fn (object $entity): array => match (true) {
    $entity instanceof Attachment => ['subject' => $entity->getSubject()],
    default => [],
});
```

### 🗂️ The audit root index

When at least one entity has roots, `audit:schema:update` creates one more table per storage, `audit_root` (with the
`table_prefix`), which indexes each audit entry under its roots:

| Column | Content |
|---|---|
| `root_class` | FQCN of the root, the root class of its inheritance hierarchy |
| `root_id` | identifier of the root |
| `root_path` | path (or resolver key) that led to the root |
| `audit_table`, `object_id`, `transaction_id` | the audit entry |
| `created_at` | date of the audit entry |

Rows are written in the same database transaction as the audit entries (batched with them when `batch_size` is set).
The roots are resolved during the flush:

- when the first association of a path changes, the entry is indexed under the **old and the new** root: moving a
  visit report to another property shows in both histories;
- the owner of an inverse `OneToOne` not set in memory is looked up among the entities being inserted or updated;
- removed entities are indexed while they still know their roots, so their history stays in the history of the root.

#### Rebuilding the index

```bash
php bin/console audit:roots:rebuild                     # every entity with roots
php bin/console audit:roots:rebuild --entity='App\Entity\VisitReport' --dry-run
```

The command replays the diffs of the existing schema v2 entries: the first segment of a path is read from the diffs
of the entry's entity, the next ones from the audit history of the entities the path goes through, as they were when
the entry was written. It writes the missing rows of the paths declared with `#[AuditRoot]` or `roots`, and never
deletes a row: it can be run again safely, and rows you write yourself (for entries whose diffs do not hold the
association, such as imported or legacy entries) are kept. Roots returned by a `root_resolver` cannot be replayed.
Run it after declaring a new root, or after migrating audit tables to schema v2
(`audit:schema:migrate --force --convert-all`): entries in schema v1 or without a transaction id
are skipped and counted. The command fails when an `--entity` is not audited, when it already runs, or when the diffs
of an entry cannot be read; in the last case the rows of the other entries are still written. Rows that no longer match the configuration (a removed path) are not cleaned up: delete
them with SQL if needed.

Index rows go with their entries: the retention pruning (`audit:clean` and the scheduled retention) deletes
the rows whose entry it deleted, and a rolled-back transaction deletes its rows from a remote storage along with its
entries.

### 📜 The history of a root

```php
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Reader;

$reader = new Reader($provider);
$query = $reader->createRootQuery(Property::class, 42);

$page = $query->fetch(20);              // RootPage
foreach ($page->group() as $item) {     // list<HistoryItem>, one per transaction
    // $item->username, $item->origin, $item->getChanges()…
}

$next = $query->fetch(20, after: $page->lastCursor);
$newer = $query->fetch(20, since: $page->firstCursor);   // entries written since the page was read
```

The query reads the entries of the root itself and those indexed under it, in every audit table concerned, and
merges them: most recent first, then by transaction id, entity and id. Each `Entry` has `$entry->entity` (FQCN) and
`$entry->rootPath` (null for the root itself).

Pagination uses opaque cursors (keyset pagination), so a page never shifts when entries are written in the
meantime. `fetch()` extends a page past its size until the transaction of its last entry is complete, so that an
action is never split between two pages: pass the `HistoryGrouper` (or key callable) you display the page with to
keep its groups whole, or `false` to cut the page at its size exactly. `iterate()` yields every entry, keyed by
cursor, reading each table by batches; `count()` counts them.

`fetchTransactions()` counts a page in transactions instead: every page but the last holds exactly that many actions,
each one whole, whatever its number of entries. `countTransactions()` counts the transactions of the history, once
each even when they wrote in several audit tables (twice when these tables are on two connections).

```php
$page = $query->fetchTransactions(20);                        // 20 actions
$next = $query->fetchTransactions(20, after: $page->lastCursor);
$total = $query->countTransactions();
```

A cursor that is not one (edited by hand in a query string, for instance) makes `fetch()` and `iterate()` throw an
`InvalidArgumentException`. `RootQuery::isCursor($cursor)` tells it beforehand, to show the first page instead:

```php
$after = $request->query->getString('after');
$page = $query->fetch(20, after: RootQuery::isCursor($after) ? $after : null);
```

#### Options

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `include` | `?list<string>` | `null` | FQCNs of the entities to read (all by default) |
| `paths` | `list<string>` | `[]` | Root paths to keep (all by default). Leaves the entries of the root itself out |
| `self` | `bool` | `true` | Read the entries of the root itself |
| `type` | `string\|array` | `null` | Operation types (`insert`, `update`…) |
| `blame_id` | `int\|string\|array` | `null` | Authors |
| `changed_field` | `string\|list<string>` | `null` | Entries that changed one of the fields (native JSON needed) |
| `blame_origin` | `string\|BlameOrigin\|array` | `null` | `http`, `console`, `messenger`, `system` (native JSON needed) |

An entity in `include` that is not audited, or a path in `paths` that no entity declares (when no `root_resolver` is
set), throws an `InvalidArgumentException`, as does a root class that no auditing entity manager maps.

Only the `view` role of the **root** is checked: reading the history of a root gives access to the entries of the
entities indexed under it. Use the `read_scope` option to restrict them further.

### 🔎 Field-level queries

```php
// last change of each field, or the creation (or snapshot) for a field never changed since
$changes = $reader->getLastChanges(Property::class, 42, ['price', 'status']);
$changes['price']?->getValue('price');  // value of the field: after the change, or at the creation (deep diff tree for a JSON field)
$changes['price']?->getLabel('price');  // its label (#[DiffLabel], association), if any
$changes['price']?->entry->username;    // who, when: the Entry of the change
$changes['price']?->entry->createdAt;

// entries that changed a field, of one object or of all objects of a class
$entries = $reader->getFieldHistory(Property::class, 42, 'price')->execute();
$entries = $reader->getFieldHistory(Property::class, null, 'price')->execute();
```

`getLastChanges()` returns `array<string, ?Change>` (null when nothing was audited). For a field never changed, the
change is the creation of the object, which holds the requested fields: read the value with `getValue($field)` rather
than `new`. For a JSON field changed since, `getValue()` returns the deep diff tree of the last change, not the whole
value (`ChangeKind::Json`). It reads the entries that
changed one of the fields when the platform has native JSON support, and scans the history of the object otherwise.
`getFieldHistory()` returns a `Query` with a `ChangedFieldFilter`, which needs native JSON support.

The `changed_field` option of `createQuery()` also takes a list of fields (entries that changed any of them), and
`blame_origin` keeps the entries of some origins (`BlameOriginFilter`).

### 🧱 Read scope

`read_scope` is a callable applied to every query the reader creates, including each table of a root query. It
receives the query and the FQCN of the entity it reads, and can add filters, for instance to keep the entries of the
current tenant (a `RootFilter` built by hand takes the root class of the inheritance hierarchy):

```php
$configuration->setReadScope(static function (Query $query, string $entity) use ($tenant): void {
    $query->addFilter(new JsonFilter('extra_data', 'tenant', $tenant->getId()));
});
```

### 🏷️ Entity labels

`entity_label_resolver` is a callable (see `EntityLabelResolverInterface`) that builds the label of an entity
written in the `source` and `target` blocks of the diffs, and in association values. Return null to keep the
default label (the string representation of the entity, otherwise `Class#id`); a `Stringable` is accepted. It runs
during the flush and must not flush: an exception it throws aborts the flush and rolls the transaction back.

### Related

- [Querying](index.md)
- [Filters](filters.md)
- [Configuration](../providers/doctrine/configuration.md)

## Querying Audits (Auditor-doctrine-provider)

> **Read and query audit entries with the Reader and Query APIs**

This guide covers how to read and query audit entries using the `Reader` and `Query` APIs.

### 🔍 Overview

The DoctrineProvider includes a querying system built on top of Doctrine DBAL:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    R["Reader"] --> Q["Query"]
    Q --> F["Filters"]
    Q --> E["Entry[]"]
```

- **Reader** — Factory for creating queries and utilities
- **Query** — Builds and executes audit queries against DBAL
- **Filters** — Filter results by various criteria
- **Entry** — Represents a single audit log entry

### 📖 The Reader Class

#### Namespace

```php
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Reader;
```

#### Creating a Reader

```php
$reader = new Reader($provider);
```

#### Creating a Query

```php
// Simple query for all audits of an entity
$query = $reader->createQuery(App\Entity\Post::class);
$audits = $query->execute();

// Query with options
$query = $reader->createQuery(App\Entity\Post::class, [
    'object_id' => 42,        // Specific entity ID
    'type'      => 'update',  // Action type
    'page'      => 1,         // Pagination
    'page_size' => 20,
]);
```

#### Query Options

| Option             | Type                    | Default | Description                               |
|--------------------|-------------------------|---------|-------------------------------------------|
| `object_id`        | `int\|string\|array`    | `null`  | Filter by entity ID(s)                    |
| `type`             | `string\|array`         | `null`  | Filter by action type(s)                  |
| `blame_id`         | `int\|string\|array`    | `null`  | Filter by user ID(s) who made changes     |
| `user_id`          | `int\|string\|array`    | `null`  | Alias for `blame_id`                      |
| `transaction_id`   | `string\|array`         | `null`  | Filter by transaction ID(s) (ULID)        |
| `changed_field`    | `string\|list<string>`  | `null`  | Entries whose diff touches this field, or one of these fields (see [ChangedFieldFilter](filters.md#-changedfieldfilter)) |
| `blame_origin`     | `string\|BlameOrigin\|array` | `null` | Entries made from these origins (see [BlameOriginFilter](filters.md#-blameoriginfilter)) |
| `page`             | `int\|null`             | `1`     | Page number (1-based)                     |
| `page_size`        | `int\|null`             | `50`    | Number of entries per page                |
| `strict`           | `bool`                  | `true`  | With single table inheritance, keep only the entries of the queried class (filter on the discriminator) |

### 📄 Executing a Query

```php
// Returns an array of Entry objects
$entries = $query->execute();

// Returns the total count (ignoring pagination)
$total = $query->count();
```

### 📃 Pagination

```php
<?php

$query = $reader->createQuery(App\Entity\Post::class);
$result = $reader->paginate($query, page: 2, pageSize: 25);

// $result contains:
// 'results'         → \ArrayIterator<int|string, Entry>
// 'currentPage'     → int
// 'hasPreviousPage' → bool
// 'hasNextPage'     → bool
// 'previousPage'    → int|null
// 'nextPage'        → int|null
// 'numPages'        → int
// 'haveToPaginate'  → bool
// 'numResults'      → int
// 'pageSize'        → int

foreach ($result['results'] as $entry) {
    echo $entry->type . ': ' . $entry->objectId . "\n";
}
```

#### Pages of transactions

A transaction (an action: the flushes of one database transaction share its id) often writes several entries, so pages of entries cut actions and hold a varying
number of them. `transactions()` pages the transactions the query reads instead, with its filters (its order and limit
do not apply), most recent first:

```php
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Filter\SimpleFilter;
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Query;

$query = $reader->createQuery(App\Entity\Post::class, ['page_size' => null]);

$total = $query->countTransactions();
$transactions = $query->transactions(limit: 25, offset: 25);   // list<TransactionSummary>, page 2

// then the entries of these transactions, with the same filters, most recent first
$ids = array_values(array_filter(array_map(static fn ($transaction) => $transaction->transactionId, $transactions)));
$entries = $query->transactionEntries($ids);                    // or transactionEntries($ids, limit: 1000)

// an entry without transaction id is a transaction of its own
foreach ($transactions as $transaction) {
    if (null === $transaction->transactionId && $transaction->table === $query->getTable()) {
        $entries = [...$entries, ...(clone $query)->addFilter(new SimpleFilter(Query::ID, (string) $transaction->entryId))->execute()];
    }
}
```

A `TransactionSummary` tells its `transactionId`, the date of its most recent entry (`createdAt`) and its number of
`entries`. Transactions are ordered by that date, then by transaction id (both descending). An entry written without
transaction id is a transaction of its own: `transactionId` is null, `entryId` and `table` identify it. A table not
migrated to schema v2 is read through its `transaction_hash` column; in a table being migrated (`audit:schema:migrate`
without `--convert-transaction-hash`), a row not converted yet stands for its transaction by its hash, as
`$entry->transactionId` does, and `transactionEntries()` reads it too.

`Query::transactionsOf($queries, $limit, $offset)` and `Query::countTransactionsOf($queries)` do the same across
several audit tables (one query per table): a transaction that wrote in several tables is one transaction. The tables
of one connection are read in one statement; across connections, each one is read for `$offset + $limit`
transactions. A transaction stored on two connections is listed once but counted twice (the last page may come out
short), and its number of `entries` only counts the part read on each connection.

When the transactions are read on one audit table (a query alone, or the only table of its connection), a page that
ends within the first 10,000 transactions walks the entries most recent first, on the `created_at` index, until it has
found them. Measured with 3,000,000 entries in 750,000 transactions, by pages of 50: page 1 in 2 to 6 ms, page 100 in
40 to 100 ms, instead of 1.3 to 25 s. A deep page with a very selective filter that the date order does not serve (one
user, anonymous entries) can be slower than grouping: up to 1.4 s instead of 75 ms on PostgreSQL. The other pages group
the entries the filters keep, in the database:
- deeper pages;
- a page whose walk reads, or would read, more than 50,000 entries (very large transactions);
- a table being migrated;
- several tables of one connection, read in one statement.

On a large table without a selective filter, such a page costs a pass over the table, and so does
`countTransactions()`.

`countTransactionsByDay()` counts the transactions the query reads by day of their entries, for an activity graph:

```php
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Filter\DateRangeFilter;

$query = $reader->createQuery(App\Entity\Post::class, ['page_size' => null])
    ->addFilter(new DateRangeFilter(Query::CREATED_AT, new DateTimeImmutable('-29 days midnight')));

$query->countTransactionsByDay();   // ['2026-11-24' => 13, '2026-11-25' => 4]
```

Days are those of the `created_at` column as stored (`DATE(created_at)`), in ascending order; days without any
transaction are left out. A transaction whose entries span midnight counts on each of its days, as a filter on either
day finds it.

### 🔎 Querying by Transaction

Retrieve all audit entries related to the same database transaction across all configured entities:

```php
<?php

// Get all entries that belong to the same transaction
$byEntity = $reader->getAuditsByTransactionId('01JH8Z6Q3C2V5W7X9Y0A1B2C3D');

// Returns: ['App\Entity\Post' => [Entry, ...], 'App\Entity\Comment' => [Entry, ...]]
foreach ($byEntity as $entityClass => $entries) {
    echo "Entity: $entityClass\n";
    foreach ($entries as $entry) {
        echo '  ' . $entry->type . ' #' . $entry->objectId . "\n";
    }
}
```

> [!NOTE]
> `getAuditsByTransactionId()` silently skips entities for which the current user does not have the `view` role.
> `getAuditsByTransactionHash()` is deprecated: it forwards to `getAuditsByTransactionId()`, which also finds the
> rows of tables not migrated yet by their legacy `transaction_hash`.

### 🔍 Filtering Examples

#### Filter by Entity ID

```php
// Single ID
$query = $reader->createQuery(Post::class, ['object_id' => 42]);

// Multiple IDs
$query = $reader->createQuery(Post::class, ['object_id' => [1, 2, 3]]);
```

#### Filter by Action Type

```php
// Single type
$query = $reader->createQuery(Post::class, ['type' => 'update']);

// Multiple types
$query = $reader->createQuery(Post::class, ['type' => ['insert', 'update']]);
```

#### Filter by User

```php
$query = $reader->createQuery(Post::class, ['blame_id' => 'user-123']);
```

#### Filter by Transaction ID

```php
$query = $reader->createQuery(Post::class, ['transaction_id' => '01HXYZ1234567890ABCDEFGHIJ']);
```

#### Advanced Filtering

For advanced filtering not covered by the `createQuery` options, add filters directly on the `Query` object:

```php
<?php

use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Filter\DateRangeFilter;
use DH\Auditor\Provider\Doctrine\Persistence\Reader\Query;

$query = $reader->createQuery(Post::class);

// Filter by date range
$query->addFilter(new DateRangeFilter(
    Query::CREATED_AT,
    new \DateTimeImmutable('2024-01-01'),
    new \DateTimeImmutable('2024-12-31')
));

$entries = $query->execute();
```

See [Filters Reference](filters.md) for all available filters.

### 📦 Working with Entries

`Entry` objects use virtual properties (not getter methods):

```php
foreach ($entries as $entry) {
    $entry->id;               // int - audit entry ID
    $entry->type;             // string - 'insert', 'update', 'remove', 'associate', 'dissociate'
    $entry->objectId;         // string - entity primary key
    $entry->transactionId;    // string|null - ULID
    $entry->extraData;        // array|null - already decoded from JSON
    $entry->userId;           // int|string|null - blame_id
    $entry->username;         // string|null - from blame JSON
    $entry->userFqdn;         // string|null - from blame JSON
    $entry->userFirewall;     // string|null - from blame JSON
    $entry->ip;               // string|null - from blame JSON
    $entry->createdAt;        // \DateTimeImmutable
}
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> `$entry->extraData` is **already decoded**: it returns `?array`, not a JSON string. Do not call `json_decode()`
> on it. Read the diffs with `$entry->getDiffs()`.

See [Entry Reference](entry.md) for a complete description.

### 🔐 Access Control

`Reader::createQuery()` automatically checks the role checker before returning the query:

```php
use DH\Auditor\Exception\AccessDeniedException;

try {
    $query = $reader->createQuery(App\Entity\Payment::class);
} catch (AccessDeniedException $e) {
    // Current user does not have permission to view Payment audits
}
```
